Omid, whose real name cannot be used, signed up to join Iran's security forces when he was 18 years old and harbored "a deep commitment to my country." At the academy, Omid told DW, cadets were under the regime's control "day and night," from their military training through the daily prayers and speeches.
"They mold the minds of the young cadets," Omid said.

Some of these recruits, Omid said, eventually rise through the ranks of Iran's security apparatus to join an elite cadre of officers who plot missions, abductions and assassinations inside and outside of Iran — and have access to unlimited resources and personnel. And, he said, he attended their meetings.

When Omid, a burly man who carries scars accumulated during his decades-long service as a commander with Iran's elite special forces, reached out in early 2026, deliberations ensued: Could he have been sent to feed DW misinformation and lies to discredit the broadcaster, whose Farsi service is officially sanctioned in Iran? Could he be trying to harm DW or its Iranian employees?

Over the course of months, journalists from DW's investigative unit and Persian department corresponded with him. Omid shared records and photos of his training, which ranged from sniper practice and surveillance to street fighting, riot control and parachuting courses. He also provided photos and videos, documents and locations of a secret monitoring center and housing compounds reserved for high-ranking members of the Iranian security forces.
United in their absolute loyalty to Iran's supreme leader, he said, a clandestine circle of high-ranking officers plot and execute the murder and abductions of the regime's opponents.

Omid's testimony offered a rare insight into Iran's powerful and opaque security apparatus — and into the lives of the men at the core of the Islamic Republic — allowing DW to piece together a picture of how the regime has maintained deeply loyal forces despite widespread protest movements, international sanctions, rising inflation and recent attacks by its two main enemies, Israel and the United States, that eliminated much of its top military and political leadership.

DW corroborated substantial parts of Omid's account with documents, photos, videos and interviews with experts. An intermediary connected the investigative team with a second high-ranking defector, whose account corroborated key details provided by Omid. Though DW confirmed both men's identities, we are withholding certain details to protect them and their families.
In the past, Iran has gone after dissidents and opposition activists abroad, including journalists.
We asked the Embassy of Iran in Berlin and the Supreme Leader’s Office to respond to our findings. The Supreme Leader's Office did not reply.
The embassy in Berlin declined to address the individual allegations, stating that "the Islamic Republic of Iran firmly rejects these allegations and the conclusions drawn from them."

As a high-ranking member of the special forces, Omid had access to the privileges the regime often bestows upon its own: From financial incentives and lucrative economic contracts for their own enterprises to special housing compounds, with their own mosques, schools and hospitals, where personal satellite dishes are banned and religious observance is enforced.

These privileges have their price, Omid said: "control, nothing but control." Officers are tightly monitored. "You're not allowed to just attend a wedding or travel," he said. "They confiscate your passport; they even decide which schools your children are allowed to attend."

The control extends to soldiers' prospective partners, who are first vetted by the regime. Even then, Omid said, he was not allowed to share the true nature of his work with his wife. That, he said, "really eats away at you."

By separating such agents from regular Iranians, the regime can keep a closer eye on its forces, said Saeid Golkar, political scientist at the University of Tennessee, who has extensively researched the command structure of the Islamic Republic's security apparatus. "They can create peer pressure and indoctrinate much more effectively," Golkar told DW.
And, Golkar said, security forces who are largely segregated from regular Iranians are less likely to balk at using force against their civilian compatriots.
A defector from Iran's intelligence agency

A month into DW's interactions with Omid, an intermediary connected us with another high-ranking defector. The man, whom we're calling Reza, worked with the Information Ministry, Iran's intelligence agency.

Like many who are recruited into the security apparatus, Reza hails from a religious family: He grinned as he showed DW a picture on his phone of himself as a young man, sporting the long beard and turban favored by the devout in Iran.
Many of his relatives, he said, still occupy prominent positions in the Iranian regime.

In the early days, he was an ardent supporter of the regime and would sometimes cry during prayers, he said, knowing that he was serving his people and the Islamic Republic and "might even die as a martyr for Islam."

Reza said he slowly turned against the regime as he witnessed the clampdown on protesters. Over the years, officers have shot, arrested and beaten Iranians protesting the country's deteriorating living conditions and strict "morality" laws.

On the evening of January 8, amid an almost total internet shutdown, security forces opened fire on Iranians protesting widespread shortages and spiking inflation. The extent of the massacre slowly came to light as images trickled out of the country documenting the regime's atrocities.

Thousands of protesters were killed across Iran. Both Omid and Reza said the mass killings which, human rights organizations report, included the shooting of unarmed protesters in hospital beds — had horrified them.
Indeed, this ongoing brutality ultimately led them to speak with DW.
Omid was adamant that he had never shot at protesters nor ordered his subordinates to do so, although DW is unable to corroborate this.
When pressed, he conceded that he had witnessed the killing of demonstrators.

Reza said the guilt he carried after having "wasted 10, 11 years serving a cruel system" compelled him to speak out despite the risk to him and his family. "The truth is: When your opponent is a regime that doesn't adhere to any moral values, you need to be prepared for anything," he said.

Omid and Reza discussed secret command centers that are central to clamping down on protests. High-ranking members of all units and agencies gather in a monitoring room where, Omid and Reza say, huge monitors on the walls display real-time feeds from countless CCTV cameras around the capital, Tehran. They say there are other such rooms around the country.

Protest marches are also monitored from above by drones. And, Reza said, "information from forces on the ground and from Twitter, Telegram and other social networks, as well as information obtained through surveillance and interception devices — all this information is collected there."
Plainclothes agents often infiltrate protest groups. Omid said such agents were sometimes used to redirect protest marches to places where security forces lie in wait.
A representative of Iran's supreme leader "had a free hand" in ordering operations from within the command center, Omid said, as well as deciding "how harshly the protesters should be dealt with."

When regular police can no longer quell demonstrations, Omid and Reza said, elite units from the Revolutionary Guard and police, often clad entirely in black, their faces hidden behind balaclavas, are sent in to finish the job.
Human rights organizations have documented the use of automatic and semiautomatic machine guns and even heavy machine guns mounted on top of pickup trucks to clamp down on protests.

"The fact that the security forces are equipped with military-grade firearms that were designed for combat situations, for responding to protests, shows that the killings of protesters in the country are intended," finds Amnesty International Iran researcher Raha Bahreini, the author of a recent report analyzing the regime's chain of command during the 2022 protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in custody.

After months of correspondence, Omid pointed DW to an outwardly unremarkable location in Shahr-e Rey, on the outskirts of Tehran: A prayer hall sandwiched between an occupational therapy practice and a pharmacy. Though the prayer hall is named Beit al Shohada, or the house of martyrs, Omid said many officers call the place Dakhme, meaning crypt or tomb.

Omid described how high-ranking officers met under Dakhme's corrugated iron roof to plot off-the-books operations that bypass government structures. He said he had attended several meetings at Dakhme "where decisions about murder are made: It's a killing machine."

Though Omid insisted repeatedly that he had only attended the meetings because he had been ordered to by his higher-ups and he had never taken part in any of the operations plotted at Dakhme, he listed murders and abductions within and outside of Iran that he said were planned there. DW could not verify these cases but found that some of the people named had indeed died under unresolved circumstances.

Several experts DW contacted knew of Dakhme in connection with a murder attempt on an adviser to a reformist president over two decades ago. Others had never heard of Dakhme. No one DW spoke with could confirm its continued operation.

Experts agree that a facility such as Dakhme is plausible. "The Islamic Republic probably feels more of a need now to have these types of groups," Miad Maleki, a former US Treasury official who until recently designed US sanctions programs targeting Iran, told DW.
Indeed, Maleki said, military operations planned covertly at Dakhme would likely give the regime plausible deniability in cases of killings.

Because of the secrecy surrounding Dakhme, much of the following is based only on Omid's accounts and the rare images DW obtained of religious ceremonies inside the hall. The secret meetings usually kick off under the guise of religious ceremonies and rituals, he said, in a large hall often adorned with green drapes and religious banners. After a communal dinner, only those in the inner circle stay.

Those who remain hand over their mobile phones, which are locked away. Then, Omid said, "seasoned specialists from Iran's special forces and intelligence operation " discuss murder and abductions late into the night.

"For these people, a person's position isn't that important," Omid said. "If they consider someone a threat to the supreme leader of the Islamic Republic, they take it extremely seriously and take action."
After each operation, Omid said, the men return to their respective roles within Iran's security apparatus, until they gather again to defend the Islamic Republic at any cost.

Around 51% of the population of the United States is female, but that is not reflected in the makeup of the US Congress, where only 28.4% of the members are women. Nevertheless, with 152 women in total sitting in the House of Representatives and Senate, the number is higher than it has ever been in the history of the United States. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also currently higher than ever before: Some 14 of them — 28% — are women.

There are a number of reasons why there are still comparatively few female representatives in the US Congress. "Some of them are structural: There are rules and processes in place in our political system that make it harder for any newcomers to break in," said Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. "Historically, women were newcomers."

Seats in the Senate only come up for election every six years. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms, but there is no limit to the number of times they can stand for reelection, so in theory they can stay in office for decades.

Also, as Dittmar pointed out, election campaigns in the US are very expensive. Women have historically been less able to access networks of rich donors — who, like many party leaders, are still most likely to be men. Leading male politicians are also more likely to recruit men to stand as new candidates. Finally, cultural biases also play a role — the "stereotypes and expectations about what women can and should do."

The elections on November 3 will decide whether more or fewer women will sit in the US Congress over the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election in the midterms. And in 36 states, the citizens will also decide who will move into the governor's mansion.
House of Representatives: Female Democrats outnumber female Republicans three to one

In the House, 125 of the 435 representatives are women. As in the Senate, and also with the gubernatorial posts, they are not evenly distributed between the two parties: There are more women among the Democrats than among the Republicans. At present, there are 95 women sitting as representatives for the Democrats, and 30 for the Republicans.

"There is a far less robust support infrastructure for women within the Republican Party," said Dittmar. She said that organizations that specifically recruit, train and fund women candidates are almost all either on the Democrat side, or nonpartisan.

"A lot of the [Republican] party leaders don't see an electoral incentive or pressure" to recruit more women, she added. Diversity is more important to Democrat voters, who place greater value on seeing women among their elected representatives.

The Republicans currently have a majority in the House of Representatives, which means that they also get to appoint the speaker, or majority leader. At the moment, the position is held by Mike Johnson. Only one woman has held this powerful post to date: Nancy Pelosi, who was the Democrats' speaker from 2007 to 2011, and again from 2019 to 2023.

Women currently constitute 27% of the US Senate — 16 Democrats and 11 Republicans. Each of the 50 states is represented by two senators. The term of office is longer in this chamber of the US Congress, and the majority of the officials here represent many more voters than the representatives in the lower house.

According to Dittmar, it's even harder for women to win a seat in the Senate. "With the Senate, it's an opportunity and timing issue," she said. Each seat comes up for election every six years. There are 100 in total, and every two years only a third of them are available. Little opportunity, then, for women who have not previously sat in the Senate to advance.

A state-wide senatorial election campaign is also more expensive than the equivalent campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives — and studies indicate that female candidates are generally less wealthy than their male counterparts.

For one senatorial candidate, the November midterms could prove historic. If the Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins in Minnesota, she will be the first Native American woman to sit in the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe, otherwise known as Chippewa, an Indigenous people from the Great Lakes region spanning the US and Canada.

Flanagan currently holds the post of lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Polls suggest that her chances are good. She has a slight lead over her rival, the Republican Michele Tafoya, previously a sports reporter and adviser to conservative politicians.

Ten of the current 14 female governors are Democrats, while four are Republicans. Six of the 14 are standing again, including Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, who was President Donald Trump's press secretary during his first term in office.

For the first time in US history, a Black woman may be elected state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Tim Walz — Kamala Harris' vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 election — is not standing for reelection. The main rivals for his seat are the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the (Black) Republican Lisa DeMuth. Meanwhile, the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is running for governor of the state of Georgia.

Dittmar doesn't think DeMuth will win in Minnesota — the state is regarded as solidly Democrat. And Klobuchar is well known among the people there; she has represented Minnesota in the US Senate since 2007.

But in Georgia, according to Dittmar, it's a different story: "That race is considered a toss-up, 50-50." Dittmar believes that Bottoms "absolutely has a chance to be the first Black woman governor." Former President Barack Obama is her most prominent supporter, while President Trump has declared his support for the Republican candidate, Rick Jackson.
This article was originally written in German.
One person dead, several injured in roller-coaster accident near Atlanta
Officials haven't yet given details about what happened on Six Flags Over Georgia ride
One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags roller-coaster on Monday afternoon in Georgia, according to police.

Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 25 kilometres northwest of Atlanta. Detectives with the Cobb County Police Department's major crimes unit are investigating.
A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully co-operating with local authorities as they investigate.
"We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today," the spokesperson said.
Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the roller-coaster. However, local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.

The roller-coaster, which was opened in 2006, reaches top speeds of about 113 km/h and heights of 61 metres, the park's website reports. During about 3-1/2 minutes, riders "navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills," according to the website.

"I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one," Lisa Cupid, chair of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners, said in a statement. She added that next of kin have been notified.
The amusement park is a major part of the county's tourism and brings in visitors from across the southeast, Cupid said.
"We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories," she said.

This death would be at least the seventh at the Georgia park, including one in 2006 in which a man had a likely heart attack on the Goliath coaster, according to the Doan Law Firm, which focuses on amusement park accidents.

It also comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain, in Southern California, announced that it is retiring its famous X2 roller-coaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. The park had settled one wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.

Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed roller-coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries, and his death was ruled accidental.
Panama declares state of emergency as powerful quake aftershocks rattle communities
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos

The government of Panama declared a state of emergency Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours. Officials did not attribute any deaths to the quakes but reported damages in all 10 of Panama's provinces and two Indigenous territories.

The 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude earthquakes on Friday toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.

The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centered about 10 kilometres southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10 kilometres.

Presidential Minister Juan Carlos Orillac announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, health-care facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, told reporters the state had reports of 27 people with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.

The civil protection agency tallied roughly 420 homes and about the same number of public schools damaged. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.

In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64 kilometres northeast of the epicenter, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government's guidance on what to do next.

"We've been here since 1 p.m. yesterday; we haven't moved," Tony Jimenez, whose home partially collapsed, said while sitting with relatives under a tent. "It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense — truly intense."
The collapsed Church of San Atanasio was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.
Images of crumbling buildings and deep fissures slicing through roads added to fears across a Latin American region battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in recent months.

Two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes roiled Venezuela's La Guaira state in June, killing more than 6,500 people and leaving 17,000 homeless. In August, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia killed at least 289 people.

The notably lower toll in nearby Panama may have been due to the country's strict building codes, especially governing construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdes, head of the Seismology Department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.
Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.

On Isla Cana, off the Pacific coast of Los Santos, approximately 300 people were evacuated because of rising sea levels and rough surf. Meanwhile, in the city of Penonome, around 150 kilometres from the capital, a shelter was housing 13 people, including five children. The earthquakes caused a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district's main square, as well as damage to the governor's office building and the Dos Continentes hotel.
In Panama City, one of the water treatment plants supplying the area operated at 20 per cent capacity on Saturday, and tent facilities with cots were set up at six hospitals.

Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region's busiest airports with more than 20 million passengers in 2025, temporarily suspended operations after the first quake but said Friday but reopened hours later.

But hundreds of travellers on major Panama-based airlines like Copa Airlines were left stranded in airports around the region. Their connections through Tocumen — one of the biggest travel hubs in the region — were cancelled or delayed. In Mexico City's airport, airline employees scrambled as families with babies were sleeping on the floor Saturday while one woman from Venezuela shouted in panic that the flight through Panama was one of the only ways she could return home to Caracas.

The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage.

The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centered in nearby Costa Rica, killed 23 people, injured 559 and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas del Toro region.
A vehicle lies crushed beneath a collapsed building after an earthquake struck Penonome, Panama, on Friday. (Aris Mariota/The Associated Press)
Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama's border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including the Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates.
Panama lies along the "Ring of Fire," a 40,000-kilometre arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world's earthquakes occur.

Messages of support and offers of assistance flooded in from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.
The U.S. Department of State on Saturday said it mobilized a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments.
The U.S. government also pledged $5 million US for humanitarian assistance.
U.S. Southern Command also said two helicopters supported by the State Department's drug-control bureau had delivered 2,000 pounds of food to Panamanian communities affected by the earthquakes.
Villages evacuated as flash flood from Budhi Gandaki river hits northern Nepal
There were no immediate reports of casualties
Residents along the Budhi Gandaki river in north central Nepal evacuated on Sunday as flash flooding destroyed homes and other structures in the area.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority evacuated villagers and warned others to move to safer areas while remaining on alert until late Sunday.
There were no immediate reports of casualties.
The disaster management agency is trying to determine the cause of the flash flood in the Budhi Gandaki river, which merges into the Trishuli river and is a key waterway near the capital Kathmandu.

Videos on social media show houses and sheds being swept away by the swollen river flowing between tall mountains. It was not immediately clear how many of the small villages in the mountainous area were impacted. Social media posts indicate the government warning prompted an evacuation in Arughat, a riverside town on the highway connecting Kathmandu to other parts of the country.
Nepal is still recovering from a devastating flood in August along the mountainous Nepal-China border that left more than 1,400 people dead and thousands more missing.

The office of Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Monday announced an end to search and rescue operations for additional victims. Authorities will instead concentrate on recovery including restoration of roads and bridges cut off by floods, particularly in remote areas where damaged infrastructure has made aid deliveries difficult.
The government estimates the rebuilding effort will cost $4.77 billion. Nearly 33,000 people have been affected and about 7,500 homes were damaged or destroyed.
Some Victorian firefighters are being threatened with legal action to force them to pay a $644 levy.
The firefighters' union says the court proceedings may be needed to help them recover debt from mounting legal costs.
Firefighters told the ABC the legal levy is to pay for ongoing action against Fire Rescue Victoria over the the firefighters' Enterprise Bargaining Agreement.
The Victorian firefighters' union is threatening legal action against its own members for not paying a $644 levy to cover its hefty legal costs.

In what some firefighters have called a "ridiculous" move, the union last year resolved to charge all members the fee to cover the union's legal bills which financial reports show ran to almost $2.3 million last financial year.
The levy is on top of union membership fees, which are more than $2,000 per year for senior firefighters.
The letters, sent by law firm Slater and Gordon, notify members who haven't paid the levy that if the matter isn't resolved, court proceedings will be commenced against them to recover the debt.
"If proceedings are commenced, in addition to being required to pay the CCF [Court Case Funding] levy, you may also be ordered to pay interest and costs," the letter says.
One union member and senior firefighter, speaking to the ABC on the condition of anonymity, said the union should be supporting members, not attacking them.
"[It's] unhelpful and detrimental to the mental health and wellbeing of our people," he said.
He also questioned whether the cost of using a legal firm to recover the debt would actually outstrip the cost of the debt itself.
A Fire Rescue Victoria (FRV) employee told the ABC they couldn't believe the union would send a legal letter to its own members, and that one recipient had been in tears over the potential action.
United Firefighters Union Victoria branch secretary Peter Marshall said in a statement the decision to impose the levy was made by members over five union meetings, and carried unanimously.
"Most members expected the request and have already paid," he said.
"No member received a legal letter out of the blue. Every one of them was contacted several times first.
"If there are any other members who have financial or other struggles, it is well known that I can be reached at any time, and their circumstances will be dealt with sensitivity and in confidence."
The union would not say how many letters have been sent, though the FRV staff member said they were aware of more than 40.
Union spends more than $10m in legal fees over six years
Over the past six years, the Victorian branch of the union has spent more than $10 million on legal fees, according to its own financial statements.

The current legal levy is to pay for ongoing action the union is taking against FRV in the Fair Work Commission over the firefighter's Enterprise Bargaining Agreement (EBA), according to firefighters who spoke to the ABC.
The parties have been unable to resolve the EBA since 2021, with FRV making the union seven separate offers over that time.
The Fair Work case is just one of several legal actions the union had underway.

The United Firefighters Union of Australia and its secretary Peter Marshall also mounted Supreme court action against the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) this year, trying to stop the public release of a report that examined former Labor ministers and Mr Marshall.

The bid ultimately failed, with the report published in August finding Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations for the 2016 firefighters EBA and was given privileged access to senior government figures.

This included holding secret meetings with the then-special minister of state, Gavin Jennings, to thrash out a deal, unknown to the then Emergency Services Minister Jane Garrett, who opposed the union's demands.
At the time the IBAC report was handed down, Mr Marshall said he did not regret anything he had done to stand up for UFU members.
The union also has several other matters against Fire Rescue Victoria in the Fair Work Commission.
Several FRV employees told the ABC that the number of legal cases being pursued by the union was a point of frustration.

"If the union and its leadership had managed its money better and had not been so litigious, the members themselves wouldn't have to stump up for these additional costs," a senior firefighter told the ABC.
It's the second time the union has charged extra fees to members on top of their dues because of the union's legal bill.
Between 2014 and 2018, it charged members $500 a year to cover the union's legal costs against the Napthine Liberal government.
The ACCC has launched legal action against 12 egg producers and suppliers, alleging they coordinated on production and supply decisions.
The consumer watchdog alleges "widespread anti-competitive conduct" has affected egg supply in Australia since at least 2020.
A spokesperson for Sunny Queen, Australia's largest egg supplier, has denied all allegations.
Australia's competition regulator has launched legal action against some of the country's biggest egg producers alleging "cartel conduct" and other anti-competitive behaviour.

Sunny Queen, the largest egg supplier in Australia, and 11 other producers and suppliers are alleged to have breached competition laws by coordinating on the production and supply of eggs since at least October 2020.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) filed civil proceedings in the Federal Court today, alleging the companies had coordinated on a range of decisions.

The ACCC alleges that since at least October 2020, egg suppliers and producers coordinated on a range of business decisions, including buying a property in Queensland to stop a rival supplier acquiring it.
The legal filing comes over a year since the ACCC launched court action against several large vegetable producers, alleging they formed a price-fixing cartel in supplying supermarket Aldi

The ACCC alleges the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on decisions about production volumes, distribution, expansion plans and culling to manage perceived oversupply in a way that likely "substantially reduced competition for many years".
ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said eggs were an important household staple, and the alleged behaviour could result in less competitive prices for consumers.
"When you have good functioning competition then you have more choice, you also have price competition so lower prices," she told the Victorian Country Hour.
"Our concern is that when parties are not competing and they start working together and consumers can ultimately miss out.
"This alleged conduct is extremely serious."
Sunny Queen is Australia's largest wholesale egg supplier, holding about one-third of the market for supply of eggs to retailers such as Woolworths, Coles, Metcash, Aldi and Costco.
The company has warehouse and distribution facilities in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia.

The proceedings involve allegations against entities including Sunny Queen, Doug Hall Poultry Pty Ltd, Alpair Pty Ltd trading as McLean Farms, Ellerslie Free Range Farms Pty Ltd and Kinross Farm Pty Ltd along with seven other companies.
The ACCC alleges Sunny Queen, Hall and McLean Farms's coordination extended to purchasing a property in Pittsworth, Queensland, to prevent rival egg suppliers acquiring it.
"We also allege this had the effect of substantially lessening competition," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said.

The competition regulator also alleged Sunny Queen restricted how many eggs its rival Kinross could sell to customers, and prevented Kinross from selling its eggs to Coles, Woolworths, Aldi, Metcash or Costco.
A spokesperson for Sunny Queen denied all allegations.
"Sunny Queen has cooperated fully with the ACCC throughout the course of its investigation," the spokesperson said.
"Sunny Queen denies the allegations and intends to defend the proceedings."

The company said the allegations related to the terms of its agreements with its shareholders and main egg suppliers in Queensland and Victoria. It said it would remain "business as usual" while the matter was before the courts.
Doug Hall Poultry, McLean Farms, Kinross Farm, Yallamundi Farms and Ellerslie Farmers have been contacted for comment.
It is the first case the ACCC has brought involving concerted practice allegations since the prohibition was introduced in 2017.
A concerted practice involves cooperation between businesses that goes beyond them acting independently in response to market conditions.
"It can involve competitors coordinating their behaviour in ways that harm competition, even if there's no formal agreement," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said.
"It can involve communication between competitors, as we allege here, a regular exchange of information … in ways that reduce independent decision-making."
The ACCC alleges that the egg industry is highly concentrated, with a small number of large suppliers and significant barriers to entry and expansion.
Eggs are an important household staple, with Australians eating an average of more than 250 each a year, according to the ACCC.
A near miss between a Jetstar flight and a vehicle on the tarmac is being investigated by authorities after a series of incidents at a north Queensland airport.
The Airbus A320 was approaching Townsville Airport from Brisbane on October 7 when the pilots noticed a white van near the edge of the runway.
The plane passed over the van with about 15 metres' clearance.
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) is investigating the near miss, which it has labelled a "serious incident".
In a statement, Jetstar said the flight landed normally and without incident.
"Safety is our number one priority, and we are working with the ATSB to understand the circumstances surrounding this incident," a spokesperson said.
Townsville Airport is owned by Queensland Airports Limited but operates as a joint user facility under an agreement with the Australian Defence Force.
Air traffic control services at the airport are provided by the Australian Air Force.

"Defence is working closely with the ATSB regarding its investigation into a runway incursion and near-collision at RAAF Base Townsville/Townsville Airport on 7 October 2026, after a vehicle entered a restricted airside area," a department spokesperson said.
"As this matter is under investigation, Defence will make no further comment at this time."
The recent near miss follows several serious incidents at Sydney Airport in recent months, including one the ATSB said was one of the most severe runway incidents in more than 20 years.
It is also the fourth incident the ATSB is investigating in or near Townsville Airport in the past two months.

On September 5, a Jetstar flight had been scheduled to take off from Townsville to Brisbane when the crew identified a performance calculation error — where the wrong numbers, settings or weight data had been used to calculate essential flight information.
In a separate incident on September 23, a Qantas flight from Brisbane to Townsville issued a mayday call due to low fuel levels after three missed landings because of poor visibility.
Meanwhile, a near-collision on October 1, about 18 kilometres west of Townsville Airport, is also being investigated as a "serious incident".

According to the ATSB investigation summary, in that incident a de Havilland DHC-8 (Dash 8) and a two-seater Aeroprakt A22LS were both in communication with the Townsville approach controller but did not see each other until they were about 1km apart.
They were about 500m apart before the Dash-8 dropped to a lower altitude to avoid a collision.
Sidney Dekker, from Griffith University's Safety Science Innovation Lab, said there was only cause for concern if there was a common cause behind the incidents.

"Once we know what the ATSB comes up with in their investigation, then we'll have a better view of the extent to which it is connected to longstanding issues at Townsville or other airports across Australia," he said.
"Before they're done with that, there's really no basis for us to speculate about the cause."
He said the near miss involving the van was "serious enough to have a closer look at" and a "fairly rare" incident.
Dr Dekker said it was reassuring that an accident had not actually happened.
"It's reassuring the system worked," he said.

'"It came down to the final line of defence — if that's how you want to put it — that the pilots saw the van and went, 'Yeah right, we're not landing where this thing is sitting'. That is exactly what the system is supposed to do."
The ATSB will hand down reports on each incident after its investigation.
A 7.7-magnitude earthquake shook the central coast of Panama on Friday, prompting tsunami warnings for several neighboring countries.

The earthquake hit around 1:56 p.m. ET, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Around three hours later, a second powerful earthquake measuring at 6.6 magnitude, struck Panama after a series of aftershocks, which registered magnitudes between 4.8 and 5.8, rippled across the southern tip of the country.
Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt.
The U.S. Tsunami Center flagged tsunami warnings for Ecuador, Colombia, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Mexico, El Salvador, Costa Rica and Peru, as well as Panama, shortly after the quake.
The initial earthquake was centered about 6 miles southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama’s southern tip, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 6 miles.
Tremors were also felt in the capital, Panama City, where buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets. The city is known for its tall skyscrapers.
Visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.

“We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re OK, though we’re very scared,” Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.”
Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos.

Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square and the Dos Continentes hotel.

No fatalities were immediately reported, but Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of Panama Civil Protection said injured people “have been transferred to educational centers, health centers, and hospital centers.”

The province of Coclé said the governor’s palace there suffered significant structural damage, but that staff members were safely evacuated. The local government also urged community members to remain calm in the quake’s aftermath.
Video aired by local news outlets showed a Catholic cathedral collapsing and part of a hotel’s facade falling onto a car in the city of Penonomé, in the central province of Coclé.
Social media videos show collapsed buildings near the site of the original quake and the aftershocks, including a hotel reduced to rubble in the tourist-friendly Playa Venao.
Panama’s National System for Civil Protection said it is monitoring for further reports of damage throughout the country.
Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire,” the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world’s earthquakes occur.

Nearby countries sent messages of support Friday afternoon. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times.”
“Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” he wrote on X.
The U.S. Embassy in Panama said it was “closely monitoring” the aftermath of the quake and accounting for the welfare of its citizens in Panama, a well-known retirement destination for Americans.
President Donald Trump said Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin would “immediately” release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel onto the global market.
Trump made the announcement on Truth Social and said the action would will help bring diesel prices down.

Since its illegal invasion of Ukraine, wide-ranging sanctions have been applied to Russia. In order to get the diesel fuel moved, the Treasury Department simultaneously announced Friday that it would be easing sanctions on Russia through April 7.

“Today, at President Trump’s direction, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market,” the Treasury Department said on X.

A document posted to the Treasury’s website said that “the sale, delivery, offloading, or importation, including importation into the United States, of diesel fuel of Russian Federation origin are authorized through 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time, April 7, 2027.

In a separate statement, Putin said that he had informed Trump of Russia’s “readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets.” Putin did not offer any specifics, however, such as when a potential release would begin or how much fuel it would entail.

Since the start of the Iran war in February, the price of diesel fuel has soared almost 70%, and economists have warned that the price hikes will have wide-ranging inflationary effects on the global economy.
In recent weeks, sharp escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war have caused diesel to spike even further, and for multiple weeks the price of diesel set repeated all-time records.
After multiple Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy assets earlier this year, the Kremlin in July imposed a diesel fuel export ban. It has since been extended through the end of October.
Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak told state news agency TASS that his country would immediately begin lifting its export ban as a result of the Trump-Putin agreement.
Trump has publicly pleaded with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop bombing Russia’s diesel refinery plants.

“The problem I have with Ukraine and Russia is that, you know, a lot of the diesel comes … from Russia, and the Russia plants are being hit by Ukraine,” Trump told reporters recently. “And I’ve asked President Zelenskyy not to hit the diesel plants.”
“That’s what’s driving it up,” Trump said, referring to the cost of diesel. Ukraine, he added, has “Got to stop.”
On Sept. 14, Trump claimed that Zelenskyy and Putin had agreed to stop targeting energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy, however, denied that he had agreed to stop targeting Russian energy assets, telling CBS News he would only stop striking oil and gas targets if Russia agreed to the same terms.
But the Kremlin has increased its targeting of Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure this summer and fall.
Just hours before Trump’s announcement Friday, Zelenskyy welcomed a delegation of U.S. senators to the presidential palace in Kyiv.
“We can only protect ourselves from this terror by working together, and we discussed how the United States can help save lives,” Zelenskyy said on social media.
“This is a matter of political will, and it is now important to show leadership and fully cut off the financial flows sustaining Russia’s war machine.”
Zelenskyy described Trump’s move to ease sanctions on diesel Friday as “an obvious weakness.”
“It plays into Russia’s hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.

This is not the first time Trump has tried to use U.S. sanctions relief for Russia to help slow rising oil prices. The Treasury Department issued a series of 30-day sanctions waivers for Russian oil on the water this spring.
But they expired and largely did not impact the trajectory of oil and gas prices, which have continued rising for months.
Diesel futures fell 4% Friday in the wake of Trump’s announcement, but they remain higher by more than 110% since the start of this year.
Likewise, the price of crude oil barely budged. Brent crude oil traded around $104 per barrel Friday, down just 0.3% on the day.
Trump’s announcement also came just as Ukrainian negotiators departed for the U.S., for a new round of talks aimed at bringing an end to the war with Russia.

Special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner had been expected to lead the discussions. It was unclear late Friday whether they would continue as planned in light of the latest sanctions waiver.

Sudan: Drought and war push Darfur and Kordofan towards famine

The risk of famine is growing in parts of Sudan already torn apart by war, as a severe El Niño drought makes life even harder in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, the UN-backed global hunger monitor warned on Monday.

In a new alert, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said fresh evidence shows malnutrition getting worse in several hotspots. Aid is not keeping up, held back by a severe lack of funding, insecurity and restricted access.
The IPC food insecurity alert index is a global partnership that includes the UN emergency food agency WFP and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

In Eastern Jebel Marra, South Darfur, a survey of two camps for displaced people found acute malnutrition among children at 38 and 30.8 per cent – above the threshold for famine. Hunger was severe and death rates were high.
Across Greater Darfur, 13 of the 17 nutrition surveys carried out since January found critical levels of acute malnutrition.
In Nyala, the share of children seeking nutrition help who needed treatment for severe acute malnutrition more than doubled between January and August, from five to 11 per cent.
Drought now covers more than half of Sudan, wiping out crops in some areas and leaving families without food or income.
In North Darfur, 64 per cent of cropland is showing poor plant growth.
Rains arrived in late September, too late to save most cereal crops, the alert said, and cereal prices are very likely to keep rising.

Greater Kordofan, described in the alert as the epicentre of Sudan’s conflict, has seen more than 300,000 people forced from their homes since October 2025. Markets have been hit by more than 170 airstrikes, looting incidents or armed clashes this year.
Aid workers face extreme danger. Two trucks contracted by WFP came under fire on 2 and 3 October, killing at least one person.

Children are going without treatment. As of August, only 26 per cent of those expected to need care for severe acute malnutrition with medical complications had received it. Without treatment, as many as two thirds of them could die.
As of 8 October, less than half of the humanitarian appeal for Sudan had been funded.
The IPC’s Famine Review Committee said there is not enough survey data for a full analysis, but the evidence points to a rapidly worsening situation.
“Famine is the collapse of systems,” the committee said. “We are witnessing a humanitarian catastrophe, already of historic proportions.”

The alert called for an end to the fighting, safe and sustained access for aid agencies – especially in North and West Kordofan – and flexible funding on a large scale. Without a major increase in help, it warned, more lives will be at risk.
Giving a dam: Cultivating peace in Côte d’Ivoire

Adam Ouattara and Makongo Traoré have four children and a home on the edge of Torla village in Côte d’Ivoire. He herds cattle. She grows vegetables on a small plot nearby. For years, the dry season pitted their two livelihoods against each other.
As grazing land and water points dried up, Mr. Ouattara and other herders have had to push their cattle farther from the village, often straight through cultivated fields.

Damaged crops led to disputes with farmers, a familiar dry-season strain across much of northern Côte d’Ivoire, where seasonal pastoral movement and expanding farmland increasingly compete for the same ground.

“When resources become scarce, everyone is trying to protect their livelihood,” said Mr. Ouattara, who has led the local herders association since 2021, representing pastoralists in disputes and community talks.
A rehabilitated agropastoral dam, completed this August, is changing that math. The dam now holds more water and releases it more reliably through the dry months, for livestock and irrigation alike.
For Mr. Ouattara, the shift shows up in fewer confrontations. “Today, we sit together and discuss,” he said. “There are fewer conflicts.”
For Ms. Traoré, it shows up in her fields. A steady water supply has let her expand her vegetable plot – work she says now supports her children’s schooling. The maths is easy.
“If we can work well in our fields,” she said, “we can provide for our children and send them to school. Before, the lack of water made life difficult.”

In a region where many herders move seasonally with their livestock, access to water plays a critical role in supporting livelihoods and fostering social cohesion between pastoralist and agricultural communities.

The dam is already helping create conditions for peaceful co-existence between herders and farmers in Torla, managed locally by the community and supported by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN Peacebuilding Fund and partners.
The goal is simple: Prevent conflicts linked to competition over natural resources and boost community resilience.
The results are already playing out in Torla, where a new chapter of community dialogue and shared resource management has begun.
For residents, this project goes beyond livestock or agriculture, representing an opportunity to build a more resilient future.
“The dam brings peace to the village,” Mr. Ouattara said. “Today, we can access water here and that reduces many of the challenges we faced before.”

For Ms. Traoré, reliable access to water means greater stability for her vegetable plot and her family. It also means new opportunities for women in the community for market gardening, an important source of household income in the area.
“Now, we have the possibility to work harder and ensure a better future for our children,” she said.
Like many communities across northern Côte d’Ivoire, Torla has witnessed changing environmental conditions in recent years.

According to Adam Ouattara, increasing pressure on land has affected traditional grazing patterns: during the rainy season, agricultural production expands, leaving less space available for livestock.
“When the cultivators grow crops, much of the land is occupied, and our animals have to move farther away, sometimes towards the borders, to find pasture,” he explained.

Such challenges highlight the importance of investments that support both farming and pastoral activities while promoting peaceful co-existence. As president of the herders' association, Mr. Outtara has witnessed significant progress through improved dialogue.
“Today, we sit together and discuss,” he said. “We approach one another to talk and understand each other. There are fewer conflicts.”
India: UN rights office urges release of ‘arbitrarily detained’ protesters

The UN human rights office (OHCHR) has voiced concern over reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, civil society members, lawyers and journalists, before and during large-scale protests in Delhi on Saturday.

The demonstration was called by a youth-led movement that is seeking electoral reforms ahead of state elections, with its chief demand being the resignation of the official heading India’s election commission.
Protesters have criticised the body’s revision of the national voter roll, which has reportedly removed tens of millions of names in a bid to avoid duplicates and discrepancies.
Political opponents argue it is an exercise to keep the ruling nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in power.
Police refused permission for Saturday’s protest to take place at the movement’s planned venue in the capital, and heavy security and road closures were reported.
Media reports say the movement’s leaders were among those detained.
UN human rights office spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan called on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is “fully respected and fulfilled”.
“Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality,” he said.
He urged law enforcement officers to show “utmost restraint” in responding to peaceful protesters, in keeping with India’s democratic traditions and its human rights obligations.
Mr. Al-Kheetan said that anyone arbitrarily detained must be released immediately and unconditionally.
He also encouraged the authorities to engage in meaningful dialogue to address what he described as broadly held concerns.

Noordwijk, the Netherlands | September 22, 2026 – During the international Industry Space Days 2026 event at the European Space Agency’s ESTEC facility in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, the Latvian Mobile Telephone (LMT) Group and the globally leading space consultancy Novaspace signed a cooperation agreement on the development of a concept for telecommunications innovation platform for Latvia to link the national connectivity sector with the international satellite industry. The initiative follows the successful ESA 5G/6G Non-Terrestrial Network Hub model and will explore Latvia’s potential role within this network.

Signing the agreement marks a pivotal step toward creating a hub for developing an internationally competitive telecommunications sector in Latvia. The hub will strategically bring LMT into the space industry and impact the emergence of a wider Latvia’s space innovation ecosystem in next-generation satellite technologies, products, and services tailored to commercial applications, resilient critical infrastructure, security, digitalization and green transition. Essentially, the hub will attract national and international cooperation, funding and talent.

The next generation of mobile communications is closely linked to the rapid growth of the space economy globally. The space infrastructure is already gradually enhancing terrestrial networks, and the 6G era of telecommunications will seamlessly link terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks. The rationale for such development is efficient and resilient connectivity, especially essential in scenarios involving severe weather, power outages or physical infrastructure disruptions.

This initiative builds upon LMT Group’s strategic expansion of its track record in connectivity innovation. LMT is already collaborating with ESA and satellite operator Sateliot to pioneer energy efficient dual-mode satellite Internet of Things (IoT) connectivity, enabled by Latvia’s associate membership in ESA. The hardware and software to be developed will cover the current market gap in devices that can seamlessly switch between terrestrial and satellite networks. The planned 5G/6G NTN hub is a natural next step in scaling LMT’s technological footprint within Europe’s space ecosystem.

“LMT has long evolved beyond traditional mobile operations into a full-scale technology innovator. As we prepare for the 6G era, integrating satellite communications into our infrastructure and service portfolio is essential. Our goal is to ensure resilient, secure communications for new commercial services and for critical infrastructure under any circumstances, to produce exportable space technologies and develop services that contribute to digitalization and green transition. Partnering with Novaspace will allow us to define Latvia’s unique value proposition within the European space ecosystem and expand local high-tech expertise,” Ingmārs Pūķis, VP & Member of the Management Board at LMT.

The agreement was signed under the EU-funded FIERCE Ecosystem Building Programme, in which LMT participates as an innovation intermediary and Novaspace provides strategic support and space-market expertise. Through the programme, Novaspace will work directly with LMT to define and validate the concept, guiding LMT towards a Latvian 5G/6G terrestrial and non-terrestrial network (TN/NTN) hub. The joint effort will focus on identifying Latvia’s distinctive regional value proposition and connecting the future hub with the wider European 5G/6G and NTN ecosystem, rather than replicating existing European initiatives.

“At Novaspace, we are delighted to partner with LMT Group through the FIERCE project. The strength of Europe’s space sector depends on active participation across all Member States, and Latvia is well positioned both to benefit from and contribute to Europe’s growing space economy. Flagship European programmes such as Copernicus, Galileo, EGNOS and IRIS² are creating new opportunities for innovation, resilient connectivity and commercial growth. Drawing on Novaspace’s global market expertise, we look forward to supporting LMT in defining a distinctive role for Latvia within Europe’s 5G/6G and non-terrestrial network ecosystem,” Gabrielle Brophy, Senior Manager at Novaspace.

The planned hub will be developed together with research and industry partners in the region. This collaborative framework will help retain and grow specialized engineering and scientific competencies in the Baltic region.

The signing ceremony in Noordwijk was attended by representatives of the European Space Agency, Novaspace, the Latvian embassy in the Netherlands, the Ministry of Education and Science of the Republic of Latvia, the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia, Novaspace in representation of the FIERCE project and LMT.
Oct. 12 (UPI) -- Actor R.J. Mitte has died at 34 in Brownsville, Texas, his representatives confirmed Monday with Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter. They did not give a cause of death.
"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist and passionate disability rights advocate R.J. Mitte," the representatives said in a statement.
Most famously, Mitte played Walter White Jr. on Breaking Bad. In the AMC drama, Walter White Sr. (Bryan Cranston) became a crystal meth dealer to pay bills after he was diagnosed with cancer.

Both Mitte and his character on the show had cerebral palsy. Mitte was an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and is listed on the board of directors of his family's organization, The Mitte Foundation.

Following Breaking Bad, Mitte appeared on episodes of Switched at Birth and Now Apocalypse and the movies Triumph and Love Me Dead, as well as in other projects. His film Talking to Strangers premiered in July.

BEIRUT, Lebanon, Oct. 12 (UPI) -- The European Union decided Monday to establish a new support mission to advise and strengthen the Lebanese Army and internal security forces for an initial period of three years.
EU Foreign Affaires Ministers agreed to launch a new European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, during a meeting in Brussels, according to an EU statement.

Kaja Kallas, high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, said the mission will advise and assist the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces to "strengthen territorial control, border security and internal security."

"Europe is invested in Lebanon's future," Kallas said, adding that with this new mission, the EU continues to support the country's institutions in "restoring full sovereignty and building lasting stability for the Lebanese people."
According to the Council of the EU, the mission will have an initial three-year mandate and comprise military and civilian pillars.

The military pillar will provide advisory support and training to strengthen the Lebanese Army's capabilities in "border security and maritime security," including intelligence, surveillance and counter-smuggling.

The civilian pillar will support the Internal Security Forces through "advisory support and specialized training" in areas such as cybercrime and anti-smuggling, as well as efforts to strengthen port security governance, including at the Port of Beirut.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the EU's decision to support the country's military and security institutions, saying it reflects "Europe's firm commitment to Lebanon's security and stability."

In a statement, Aoun said the EU's new mission would help strengthen the capabilities of Lebanon's legitimate institutions, extend the state's authority across its entire territory, and secure its borders, in line with the government's decisions on restricting weapons to legitimate security forces.

The EU decision comes as Lebanon seeks to strengthen state control over its territory and disarm Hezbollah, while the mandate of the United Nations peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon, or UNIIFIL, is to expire at the end of this year.
Oct. 12 (UPI) -- The NFL suspended San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw for one game for unsportsmanlike conduct in Week 5, the league announced Monday.
Greenlaw's suspension stems from an incident that occurred in the second quarter of the 49ers' 32-29 win over the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday in Seattle.
A source told NFL Network that Greenlaw plans to appeal the suspension.
The veteran linebacker performed a headbutt -- while wearing his helmet -- on Seahawks linebacker Ernest Jones IV, who was not wearing his helmet, on the Seattle sideline Sunday at Lumen Field.
Greenlaw drew a personal foul and was ejected for the incident, which occurred after he delivered a late hit on Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold.
Greenlaw totaled three combined tackles against the Seahawks. He logged 37 combined tackles and a forced fumble through his first five starts of 2026.
He is not eligible to return until Oct. 20. The 49ers will host the Washington Commanders on Oct. 19 in Santa Clara, Calif.
In September, the Antarctic ozone hole peaked at 10.6 million square miles—the second largest ever observed for this time of year.

Using data from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, scientists found that the ozone hole started growing earlier than usual in August. By September 20, it reached a size close to its October 2015 peak, when it was 10.8 million square miles.

To understand what’s happening, we first need to understand the ozone layer. The ozone layer lies in the Earth’s stratosphere and protects our planet from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation that can harm humans, plants and animals. The infamous ozone hole is actually a patch of depleted ozone in the stratosphere over Antarctica that is mainly caused by chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs. While the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out the use of CFCs globally, they can persist in the atmosphere for decades.

The ozone hole’s size fluctuates every year. For about three months each fall—the Southern Hemisphere’s spring—the hole opens inside the stratospheric polar vortex, a large band of fast-spinning westerly winds that encircles Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. The vortex traps freezing air inside and leads to the formation of polar stratospheric clouds, writes a New Zealand-based research team in The Conversation. “Chemical reactions on particles in this rare type of cloud then activate ozone-depleting gases,” they add.

This year brought a stronger and colder polar vortex. “We have unusually strong winds and cold temperatures over the pole that have created the conditions possible for the hole to grow to the size it has today,” research team member Hannah Kessenich, a physicist at the University of Otago in New Zealand, tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC News). By late January, the hole will shrink again.
Did you know? Wildfires can destroy the ozone layer

- Climate change has increased the frequency of wildfires, which is not a good thing when it comes to mending the ozone layer. A study published in Nature in 2023 found that particles in wildfire smoke spark chemical reactions in the atmosphere that break down ozone.

So, should we be worried? “This year’s ozone hole shouldn’t be a cause for alarm,” Kessenich told Live Science's Sascha Pare in an email. “However, there are still many unanswered questions. It’s something we need to keep a close eye on.”

Kessenich and other experts underscore the fact that the ozone hole size we’re currently seeing isn’t a sign that the Montreal Protocol isn’t working. “We look at the depth of the hole rather than the area to assess how we’re coming along in terms of the recovery from those chemicals,” Kessenich says to ABC News.

In fact, this year’s hole isn’t as deep as it has been in previous years, and year-to-year variability is to be expected. “We have to look at the longer term trends, and those metrics continue to tell us that the ozone hole is slowly recovering as expected,” adds Susan Solomon, an atmospheric chemist at MIT, in an email to Live Science.

There will, however, be impacts on weather across the Southern Hemisphere. A larger ozone hole shifts the Southern Annular Mode into a positive phase, which affects winds and precipitation in different areas. In Australia, for example, it causes increased rainfall on the country’s southeast coast, Kessenich and her colleagues write in The Conversation.

Researchers are still trying to understand how climate change impacts the strength of the polar vortex, and why bigger ozone holes are persisting longer than they used to. It could be that changes in global atmospheric dynamics are making longer-lived ozone holes more likely, which in turn could mean our timelines for ozone recovery need to be adapted.
“It's too soon to tell what has been driving dynamical variability in recent years, but more research is needed,” Kessenich says to Live Science.

Historians have long known that Lismore, a small isle in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland, was home to a medieval monastery called Lios Mòr. Written records detail its sixth-century founding by St. Mo Luóc, one of the early monks who spread Christianity to northern Britain. But with very little archaeological evidence, apart from a broken granite cross, scholars could not confirm Lios Mòr’s size, style or significance—until now.

According to an article published in the journal Antiquity last week, a group of local volunteers led by archaeologist Clare Ellis, of the firm Argyll Archaeology, discovered an early medieval cemetery, various structures and “sophisticated craftworking of international importance” during excavations near Lismore’s 13th-century parish church.

“For centuries, Lismore’s early monastery was known mainly from written records and local tradition,” study co-author Gordon Noble, an archaeologist at the University of Aberdeen, says in a statement. “We can now see that it was a thriving center of worship, craftsmanship and learning, whose importance may have rivaled some of the best-known monasteries in early medieval Britain.”

Lismore’s historical society began searching for the site of Mo Luóc’s monastery in 2016. A “dynamic minority” of the island’s 170 or so residents crowdfunded and ran the digs, Robert Hay, a retired local scientist and dig participant, tells the Guardian’s Esther Addley. Grants, donations and yet more crowdfunding enabled the enthusiastic locals to hire Ellis to lead excavations near the site of Lismore’s 13th-century church, which still holds services.

“The research aimed to determine whether the site of the later medieval cathedral at Lismore was also the location of Mo Luóc’s early monastery, and to assess the scale, nature and status of the settlement,” Ellis says in the statement.

The dig uncovered a medieval cemetery containing at least six burials radiocarbon dated to between 650 and 1040 C.E. The archaeologists also unearthed a piece of an “early medieval cross slab,” per the study. In another area, they found more human remains and additional fragments of carved stone crosses.

“This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment,” Noble tells the Guardian. He compares it to Scotland’s famed Iona monastery, which was founded in 563 C.E. Both settlements were products of a medieval missionary movement that aimed to spread Christianity throughout pagan Britain. The monks succeeded. By the seventh century, Britain was Christianized.

Elsewhere on the cathedral property, researchers found the remains of an oval-shaped building paved with a layer of limestone. Dated to between the seventh and tenth centuries, it contained remnants of craftwork, handmade pottery, struck flint and an antler.

Another trench boasted extensive evidence of precious metalwork: more than 1,000 pieces of debris, including well-preserved molds and crucibles once used to melt down and cast gold, copper and silver. Hay describes them as “the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland,” per the Guardian.

Clay molds and crucibles are “unusual” finds for a monastic site, Noble tells Scientific American’s Jackie Flynn Mogensen. “It’s one of the largest metalworking assemblages we have from any site, secular or sacred, in this time period,” he adds.

The Lismore monastery appears to have an unusually large footprint. This, coupled with evidence of precious metals and craftsmanship, suggests the community was actually considerably wealthy and “far more than a small island church,” per the statement.
As Noble says to Scientific American, Lios Mòr appears to have been “a very significant mover and shaker” in its day. “It’ll be really exciting to see what shows up in the coming years.”

From soft peeps to piercing calls, birds produce a wide range of sounds. But scientists recently discovered that two South American species take their calls to ear-splitting extremes, making deafening vocalizations on par with a jackhammer.

The bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema can produce sounds at amplitudes that exceed 120 decibels, according to a study published September 29 in the journal Evolution. They’re now among the ranks of the white bellbird, another South American species, for the loudest known birds on the planet.

Researchers behind the new work didn’t specifically set out to find the world’s noisiest birds. Rather, they wanted to take advantage of recent technological advancements that have made it easier to measure vocal amplitude, the height of a sound wave and a key element of loudness.

“Until recently, it was very impractical to go out into the field and measure amplitude,” lead author João Menezes, an evolutionary biologist who conducted the research while at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, tells the New York Times’ Taylor Mitchell Brown. “It’s kind of stepping into a whole new world.”

The researchers started the project in Amherst, Massachusetts, during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when the unusually quiet circumstances made it easier to isolate and record bird song. They used a laser rangefinder to measure their distance from a specific bird, as well as a sound level meter, which allowed them to isolate that bird’s call from other noises.

“Even recording from my window or from the backyard, almost always that would be [the amplitude of] a new species,” Menezes tells the Washington Post’s Meghan Bartels. “It’s not often that you get to do this kind of exploratory science where you just go out into the field and document things for the first time, especially with birds.”

From Massachusetts, they headed next to Brazil, where they recorded birds in several different habitats. The scientists ultimately collected amplitude data on 123 bird species between December 2018 and January 2025, filling a major gap in scientists’ understanding of how loud birds can sing. Previously, scientists only had amplitude data for ten of those species—even the ubiquitous Canada goose had never been measured.

“We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” study co-author Jeffrey Podos, also an evolutionary biologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, says in a statement. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale.”

Their amplitude database captures the impressive range of bird vocalization volumes. At the low end, they documented the dusky-throated hermit, a hummingbird that buzzes at a modest 64 decibels, about the same volume as a normal conversation. At the high end, the bare-throated bellbird and red-legged seriema are both about as loud as a trumpeting elephant or a chainsaw.

Comparing the amplitude data with the birds’ anatomy revealed that species with bigger bodies and wider mouth openings also tended to be the loudest. This is probably because “bigger birds have bulkier muscles, which are capable of creating greater internal pressures, which ultimately generate louder sounds, and then broader mouths allow more energy to radiate into the environment,” Menezes tells CNN’s Amarachi Orie.

Still, the researchers have many unanswered questions. The big one: Why are some birds so much louder than others? The researchers hypothesized that the loudest birds evolved their high-volume calls to attract numerous mates, or to communicate through dense vegetation. But those explanations don’t hold up for the red-legged seriema, so there must be some other factor driving the evolution of its loud vocalizations.

“The seriema is the opposite of those two things,” Menezes tells WBUR’s Barbara Moran. “It’s a super open-habitat bird, like pasture, and it’s strictly monogamous. So, it forms a pair for the breeding season, and that’s it.”

There’s no single answer to the question of which species holds the title of “world’s loudest bird”—it depends on how researchers define loudness. The bare-throated bellbird, for example, produced the loudest individual call, reaching nearly 131 decibels, per CNN. But when researchers averaged the loudest calls across individual birds, the red-legged seriema came out on top at nearly 121 decibels. Averaging the vocalizations’ peak volumes, on the other hand, allowed the white bellbird to take the lead at 127 decibels.

Scientists are still unraveling the evolutionary underpinnings of super loud birdsong. But in the meantime, their work could have important implications for conservation. For example, reliable amplitude data could help researchers use audio recordings to determine not just whether a species is present, but also how close those birds might be and how many individuals are nearby, Connor Wood, an ornithologist at Cornell University who wasn’t involved in the study, tells the Washington Post.
The findings could also help scientists better understand how birds may adapt to a changing world.

“Amplitude is so critical to the ability of birds to communicate with each other, that it is really important for us to understand exactly how that might be able to change,” Nathan Senner, an ornithologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst who also wasn’t involved with the study, tells WBUR. “How they evolve is really fundamental to our understanding of how they might continue to evolve as our world changes.”
