Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has told the Shura Council that the region has faced “exceptional events”, following months of instability amid the United States-Israeli war on Iran.
Speaking in the Qatari capital, Doha, on Tuesday morning, Sheikh Tamim said the events had demonstrated the strength and cohesion of the country’s state institutions.
“Our country and the region have faced exceptional events that have once again proven the cohesion of state institutions,” the Emir said.

Qatar has found itself caught up in the war, which began on February 28 and has triggered a global energy crisis. The Gulf state has been directly attacked by Iran on several occasions, including in March, when Tehran struck Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas facility, the world’s largest liquefied natural gas (LNG) production site.

Sheikh Tamim said Qatar had been able to absorb the consequences of the regional instability due to policies implemented before the war, stressing that Doha’s preference was to resolve conflicts through peaceful means and dialogue. However, the Emir maintained that the Gulf Cooperation Council’s (GCC) security was non-negotiable.
“The security of the Gulf Cooperation Council states and the preservation of their sovereignty is a matter that cannot be compromised on,” he said.
The war on Iran has disrupted global supply routes, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has effectively blocked since the start of the conflict.
Sheikh Tamim said efforts to safeguard maritime routes must be increased.
“Efforts must be doubled to secure navigation in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz and to protect energy facilities and civilian infrastructure.”

Firefly, a Malaysian low-cost airline, has extended the suspension of its flights between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore through Wednesday as smoke from fires in Indonesia continued to blanket the region.
The announcement came as IQAir, an air quality monitor, ranked Singapore and the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur as the world’s two most polluted cities on Tuesday.

Firefly said in a statement that flights between the Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport (SZB) near Kuala Lumpur and the Seletar Airport in Singapore (XSP) have been cancelled up to Wednesday due to “weather and haze conditions”.
It called the action a “proactive safety measure”.

The fires, mostly on the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Borneo, are the country’s most intense in 11 years. They have been spurred by El Nino, a weather pattern expected to be among the strongest in four decades.

IQAir, a Swiss air quality monitoring company, said Air Quality Index in Singapore stood at 199 on Tuesday and 183 in Kuala Lumpur. Readings above 150 are generally considered unhealthy, and those above 300 are classified as hazardous.
Firefly, a subsidiary of Malaysia Aviation Group, which includes Malaysia Airlines, first announced the flight cancellations on October 10, citing “low visibility” due to the haze conditions.
Firefly said that affected passengers were being rebooked on Malaysia Airlines flights between Kuala Lumpur International Airport and Singapore’s Changi Airport, subject to seat availability.
The Singapore government has reintroduced subsidised care for haze-related illnesses, as it last did in 2015, when smoke from Indonesian fires hung over the region for weeks.
In Malaysia, schools reopened in most states on Tuesday as air quality improved slightly, but they remain closed in three states, one federal territory and several districts.

Malaysia’s foreign minister, Mohamad Hasan, said on Monday that he would press for stronger regional mechanisms when foreign ministers of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meet next month.

“We already have an ASEAN mechanism for natural disasters, but haze is not included or classified as a natural disaster,” he told reporters in Sepang, according to Bernama, Malaysia’s state news agency.
The Philippines, which chairs the bloc this year, confirmed that the issue would be on the agenda.
“It’s in the agenda,” Dominic Xavier Imperial, a spokesman for the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs, said of the November meeting, which will precede the 49th ASEAN summit in Manila.
Mohamad, the Malaysian minister, said Indonesia had deployed about 60,000 personnel to fight the fires, but thick smoke had grounded 34 aircraft, including planes and helicopters.

Remote terrain and limited water supplies have also hindered the effort, he said, and cloud seeding is not possible without suitable rain clouds. He acknowledged Indonesia’s efforts but urged more effective action, citing the toll on Malaysian communities.

Islamabad, Pakistan — The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party of jailed ex-Prime Minister Imran Khan is planning to legally challenge the federal government’s Sunday takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, a province that the party governed.

Sheikh Waqas Akram, the PTI’s central information secretary, told Al Jazeera that the party would challenge the imposition of emergency laws — suspending civil liberties — and governor’s rule in the province in court on Tuesday. A petition had been drafted by a legal committee headed by PTI secretary general Salman Akram Raja, but Akram did not say whether it would be filed in the Supreme Court or the Federal Constitutional Court.

The federal government’s moves have emerged as Pakistan’s latest political flashpoint, with competing narratives from the government and the PTI, at a time when the party was in the middle of a delayed march towards Islamabad, aimed at pressuring authorities to release former PM Khan, who has been in incarceration for more than three years.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday justified the government’s moves by arguing that federal rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was needed for Pakistan to effectively combat “terrorism” in the province that shares a porous border with Afghanistan.
“No war can be won, however many resources you bring, whatever you do, until the government there leads it,” Naqvi said in Peshawar on Monday.
On Sunday, President Asif Ali Zardari imposed emergency rule and governor’s rule, suspending the PTI government in the northwestern province. The party has governed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since 2013.

Sohail Afridi, the suspended chief minister, and some members of his cabinet have been taken into preventive custody, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry confirmed on Monday. Afridi had been leading the march towards Islamabad seeking to free Khan, and despite the setbacks to the party, PTI leaders said the protest was still on.
“The long march has not ended. But a historic crackdown against the party has begun,” Akram said.
According to the proclamation signed on Sunday, the provincial government had “failed to demonstrate the ownership, will and intent to adequately deal with the menace of terrorism”.

“The federal government’s position is clearly described. ‘A deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’ as communicated after cabinet meeting. That’s the constitutional premise needed for imposition of emergency,” Aasiya Riaz, joint director of the independent political think-tank the Pakistan Institute of Legislative Development and Transparency (PILDAT), told Al Jazeera.
However Hassan Abdullah Niazi, an adjunct faculty member at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a lawyer based in Lahore, disputed that premise.

“If all of this was true then KP would be in a state of anarchy, but we know that is not the case. It had a functioning legislature and executive that commanded the confidence of the people, hence this entire exercise is an unconstitutional move against provincial autonomy,” he told Al Jazeera.

A more detailed case was set out last month in a 14-page white paper presented in Islamabad by Ikhtiar Wali Khan, a political advisor to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif from the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PMLN).
The paper pointed to rising police deaths, staff and equipment shortages in the provincial counterterrorism department, and spending priorities.
However, Akram rejected the charge that the PTI had failed to lead the fight.

He said the provincial government had paid 1.83 billion rupees ($6.6 million) from its own funds to the families of more than 900 soldiers, police and paramilitary personnel killed fighting armed groups, a contribution he said no other province had made.
Naqvi said at a news conference in Islamabad on Sunday that the federal government had been involved in negotiations with the PTI on a proposed “sit-in” by the party in support of Khan.

“We have no problem with the sit-in. Do the sit-in as eagerly as you like, we have no issue with the sit-in. Our issue is entirely terrorism-related, and we want to get you on board on that,” he said.
Taimur Jhagra, a PTI leader and former provincial finance minister, also said the talks with the government that the party had agreed to were meant to focus on Khan.
“It’s absurd that a negotiation about a protest movement to give Imran Khan Supreme Court-ordered medical and visitation rights becomes a negotiation about terrorism strategy,” he told Al Jazeera.
Naqvi also said the PTI had agreed during the talks that emergency rule should be imposed in 12 districts of the province.
Akram rejected that claim and said the party had refused. The party feared residents would bear the cost of military operations, he said.
“We said ‘No, this cannot be. You cannot do whatever you like with them. We took the votes from them. Tomorrow they will blame us: you got us killed’,” he said.
Akram said the PTI negotiators referred the federal government’s proposal to Afridi, who rejected it.
Federal Information Minister Attaullah Tarar went further at Sunday’s news conference.

“This government, which has been suspended through a constitutional option, is responsible for the deaths of thousands of citizens of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa,” he said, accusing Afridi’s PTI government of being hand in glove with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan — an armed group known as the Pakistani Taliban — and the Afghan Taliban.
There is no known — leave alone public — evidence of any such links.
According to a government white paper, 122 police personnel were killed in the province in the first half of this year, up from 63 during the same period in 2025.

Independent trackers also point to rising violence. The Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), an Islamabad-based think-tank, recorded 556 violence-linked deaths in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa between July and September, up from 475 in the previous quarter and 311 in the one before.
Balochistan was hit harder. Deaths there rose by 213 percent to 829, making it the worst-affected province, according to CRSS.
The government says it acted because the provincial administration would not lead the fight against armed groups, but analysts disagree over the takeover’s purpose.
“I would say this decision is political, administrative and security. All three elements are present in it,” Zaigham Khan, an Islamabad-based political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
Ali Arqam, a longtime observer of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, disagreed.
“This is not really about security at all. It is basically a political move that they are just dressing up as some kind of administrative necessity,” he told Al Jazeera.
Jhagra said the government believed the takeover would break the PTI, but argued that people across the country still saw Khan as their leader.
“It is trying to solve for legitimacy,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to the government.
For his part, federal law minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said at a news conference in Islamabad on Sunday that the decision was a purely constitutional step.
For the PTI, the immediate concerns are its leaders and the courts.
“There has been no contact. No one in the party has had any contact with the chief minister,” Akram said.
But the party remains widely popular — in the province and nationally.
At Monday’s meeting, Naqvi said results against “terrorism” would not come in a day. There would be ups and downs, he said, and harder times lay ahead.
But Arqam, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa observer, said Islamabad should be judged by the same measures as the PTI government.
“You test this government by looking at the exact same hard metrics: Does security actually improve, do the basic services get better, and do the promised fiscal resources finally show up?” he said.
At least 72 workers were killed in air strikes on a disputed border area between Sudan and Egypt that targeted artisanal gold miners, a human rights group said Sunday.
The attack, south of the remote Halayeb triangle, east of the River Nile, is the second of its kind this year.
It comes amid growing concern in Egypt over large-scale displacement from the three-and-a-half-year conflict in Sudan, which has spurred a cross-border exodus.
The Sudan-based Emergency Lawyers, a human rights and legal advocacy organization, said the attack occurred on Saturday in rugged and mountainous territory that it said lies within Sudan.
The Halayeb triangle, which is claimed by both Egypt and Sudan, is known for mining and the gold trade, along with other illicit goods and human trafficking.
The rights group accused the Egyptian air force of carrying out the strikes.
"The repeated attacks on the gold- and mineral-rich border regions reflect a desire by Egyptian authorities to expand and assert control over Sudan's natural resources," it claimed.
Egypt has yet to comment on the strikes, but has previously admitted conducting a "large-scale operation" against illegal gold mining within its borders.
Independent verification remains difficult because of the remote location.

Sudan Doctors Network warned on Facebook of an expected increase in the number of casualties "due to the severity of some injuries and the difficulties in accessing medical care and essential services in the region."
One survivor told the AFP news agency there were thousands of people working at the remote site when it was hit.
"After the air strike, people scattered. Some people came to Al-Ansary [gold] market, others went in the other direction. That's why no one knows exactly how many were killed," he said.
Sudan's civil war between Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's military junta and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has killed more than 200,000 people and triggered a severe humanitarian crisis.
Despite backing Sudan's army chief al-Burhan, Egypt considers the war at its border a threat to its security.

The RSF has funded its operations by smuggling thousands of tons of gold from Sudan's Darfur and Kordofan regions. According to the UK-based think tank Chatham House, as much as 60% of unofficial gold exports end up in Egypt.
In June, air strikes on mining sites in the same border area were followed by a large-scale Egyptian security operation.
Hundreds of people, including foreigners, were arrested, accused of illegal gold mining and smuggling.

Pavlo Oliynyk, 25, says he joined enemy forces to escape Russian captivity. Before his capture in the Donbas region in 2024, he was a senior lieutenant for Ukraine's armed forces.

As a prisoner of war (POW), he says he was electrocuted, beaten and psychologically tortured. So when he received the offer to join the Maksym Kryvonis battalion — named after a famous 17th-century Cossack commander — he accepted.
Oliynyk says he wanted to use this opportunity to reach the front lines, so he could escape to Ukrainian-controlled territory. DW was able to contact Oliynyk through his lawyer.
'Ukrainian volunteers' consist mostly of POWs

Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former service members of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022. Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."

Of the individual units, the Maksym Kryvonis battalion has perhaps drawn the most public attention for having evidently taken part in combat. Its true size is unknown — Russian media reports claim about 200 fighters while available footage only suggests several dozen.

An investigative team of the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne has identified over 30 members and confirmed they are all former Ukrainian servicemen, captured by Russian forces between 2023 and 2024.
An 'imitation' of Russian legions fighting for Ukraine

Pavel Luzin, an expert for Russian foreign policy and defense at the Center for European Policy Analysis, believes these units are an "imitation" of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion — units in the Ukrainian armed forces, consisting of Russian citizens — and an attempt by Moscow to distract from the fact that these units exist in the first place. Ukrainian intelligence services tend to agree.

"It bothers them that Russians would fight on Ukraine's side, but Ukrainians won't fight on Russia's side," Yevhen Shybalov, author and veteran of the war in Ukraine, told DW. He added that Russian troops have never tried to hide the fact that Russian volunteer units in Ukrainian ranks were the main reason Russian forces wanted to create Ukrainian units for their own ranks.
Just how voluntary are these combat units?
In 2025, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported that 95% of the released Ukrainian POWs interviewed reported torture or ill-treatment during Russian captivity.

Bill Wiley, executive director of the NGO Commission for International Justice and Accountability, said the physical and psychological state of the returned combatants raises serious doubts that their recruitment was voluntary. Mykhailo Savva of the Center for Civil Liberties, a Kyiv-based human rights organization, points to the criminal procedures running against several of the battalion members, which he said indicates that these suggest the combatants had switched sides voluntarily.

But where to draw the line between voluntary and involuntary recruitment? The war veteran and human rights activist Maksym Butkevych, who spent 28 months as a prisoner of war, said the conditions in Russian captivity make that line hard to distinguish. On the one hand, he said, there is a constant atmosphere of pressure, and on the other hand, it's not implausible that some prisoners defected out of ideological proximity.
How were Ukrainian prisoners made to join Russian forces?

Butkevych told DW that between 2022 and 2023, all Ukrainian prisoners of war had received offers, "more or less persistently," to join the Russian army. In his case, he recounted, it was after he had been severely mistreated.
"They showed us they could do anything they wanted to us," he explained, "which was why we should agree to everything."

The veteran Shybalov reported similar experiences, speaking of attempts to force confessions of war crimes, or to recruit members for Russia's intelligence services. He told DW all prisoners were first interrogated and then made certain propositions under duress.

"You can torture people to get them to confess, but there comes the difficult moment when you need to give them a weapon," he said. "That's why it's more about psychological pressure, and forcing voluntary compliance."
Butkevych confirmed these accounts with his own tales. But neither veteran has ever met someone willing to join Russian units, they said.
Oliynyk, from the Maksym Kryvonis battalion, said he initially turned down multiple bids to join Russian forces. He said he only accepted the fourth offer so he could flee.

He claimed he didn't sign official Defense Ministry paperwork, but a private contract with an individual offering military services. Afterwards, he said, he was brought to a room where he heard lectures and saw videos and photos he was later asked to retell.
Oliynyk said fellow service members in the Maksym Kryvonis battalion consisted both of those who had switched sides of their own volition, and those who had been forced.

In a video circulating online that appears to be of a trial in Ukraine, he also says former Ukrainian POWs in the unit were followed and guarded by mercenaries of the private Russian military company Redut. In the same video, he also speaks of beatings and torture, and receiving monthly wages in envelopes handed out by a member of Russia's military intelligence.

Oliynyk told DW he had been given a phone, but that he was too scared to call anyone in Ukraine because it was under constant surveillance. He denied having fought against Ukrainians, as he fled in March 2025 before his first deployment in the Donetsk province. After running across a field, he said he spent two days hiding from drones in basements and houses before making contact with Ukrainian fighters.
Now, Oliynyk has been in detention in Ukraine for nearly two years while authorities investigate possible treason. He has yet to be formally charged.
Sergey Nikitin contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Ukrainian.
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," the president wrote on his Truth Social network.
Trump continued: "Both parties have agreed," before urging restraint from both Kyiv and Moscow: "Do not break it!"
Zelenskyy: Energy ceasefire 'news for me'
There was no immediate confirmation from Moscow, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's post that the ceasefire was "news for me."

"The ceasefire announcement was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree. If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins; we are ready and we will accept it," he told Axios.
In a social media post later, Zelenskyy said a drone had hit a Kyiv power plant, leading to power outages in the capital.
The Ukrainian leader had earlier repeated his stance that Ukraine would stop hitting Russian oil refineries if the Kremlin curbed its energy attacks.
Trump and Zelenskyy have argued this week over Ukraine's attacks on Russian diesel facilities, which the US president said have contributed to a global diesel shortage, rather than the Iran war.
Trump needs lower fuel prices before midterms
Trump said Friday he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia.
The controversial move was an attempt to bring down high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections next month.
However, this move undercuts fresh US sanctions Trump signed just weeks ago to further hurt Russian energy revenues funding the war.
On Sunday, a bipartisan group fo six US senators called on the Trump administarion to "immediately reverse course" and scrap the diesel deal.

The signatories included Democrats Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, and Republicans Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the senators said in a joint statement.

Backing Zelenskyy in the Trump row, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that she "fully supported" the call for a "ceasefire that protects global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia."
"And my full support for President Zelenskyy as he leads the fight for his people's freedom," she wrote online.

On X, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his country "strongly supports" Trump's call for a "sustained energy ceasefire to start now," which he said Kyiv was ready to honor "if Russia stops its attacks."
French President Emmanuel Macron said his country backs a "real energy ceasefire," but lamented that "Russia continues to refuse that."
After earlier denouncing the Trump-Putin deal, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he supported the energy ceasefire, in a phone call with Trump, his office said.
Russia has repeatedly struck Ukraine's power plants and transmission lines around Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa and elsewhere, to lower civilian morale, especially during the winter months.
Recently, Ukraine has stepped up long-range strikes deep inside Russian territory, targeting major oil refineries and other facilities to curb Moscow's refining capacity and fuel supplies.
Kyiv on Sunday pressed on its campaign against Russian infrastructure, hitting a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex.
It was the third strike on the company's facilities in four days.
Judge orders Trump administration to end taxpayer-funded TV ads
Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million US in taxpayer money for ads

U.S. President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the non-partisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads and called them an illegal misuse of funds.
In granting a temporary restraining order, she told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night.

The White House did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment on Sunday night. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow."

The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million US in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested they ran afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda" and potentially other federal laws.
The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175-million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump's immigration enforcement agenda.
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies.

But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren't aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs. One of the ads is a near replica of a 2024 ad that Trump ran during his presidential re-election campaign.
Hurricane Simon hits Mexico's Pacific coast, slamming towns and resorts
Hurricane specialist says 'life-threatening' storm surge expected

Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.

The hurricane's centre swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning.
Its maximum sustained winds weakened late Sunday to 185 kilometres per hour, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami, but it was still expected to remain a dangerous hurricane.

That's not good news for people in the Puerto Vallarta area, a popular destination for Canadian tourists. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.

By late Sunday, Simon's eye was moving northwest about 75 kilometres south of Cabo Corrientes at about seven kilometres per hour. A senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system.
Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific.
"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said.
- Category 4 Hurricane Simon barrels toward Mexico
- Hurricane Simon forecast to get much stronger as it heads to Mexico's Pacific Coast

As for predicting whether or not Simon will make landfall, "it's a little tricky right now" to forecast, since the eye "is basically moving very close or parallel to the coast currently," Pappin said.
People watch waves crash against the waterfront promenade in Puerta Vallarta on Sunday as Hurricane Simon approaches. (Christian Ruano/Reuters)

Meanwhile, the hurricane was dumping rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 25 to 50 centimetres of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 76 centimetres. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the centre warned.

As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers as well as visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.
On Saturday, just ahead of the worst weather, convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows.
A man removes water from a building in Manzanillo on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)

The hurricane centre expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the centre makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.
Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who, along with his wife, still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.
"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do. "I just don't know what to expect."
Children among at least 139 dead after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti coast
Toll only includes those buried by authorities, says UN migration agency

At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in East Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday.

That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves, but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, told The Associated Press.
"What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation," Coissac said. "They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened."
Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, "mainly because it was overcrowded."
"The local authorities did their best," Coissac said, "but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore."
He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue centre in Obock where they would receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support.
A pair of trousers believed to belong to a migrant lies on the shore near Guhere. (Kennedy Omondi Okoth/International Organization for Migration/Reuters)
"They're all in a state of shock," said Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday. "I tried to talk to some of them, but it's very difficult."

Some of the migrants in the IOM centre are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive.

At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.
The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said.
The Geneva-based UN migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise.
Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing.

Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait toward Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement.
That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait.
"This is a devastating loss of life," said Coissac. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."
Members of the International Organization for Migration receive migrants near Guhere. (Kennedy Omondi Okoth/International Organization for Migration/Reuters)

In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: the tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia.

Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project.

"No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," IOM director general Amy Pope said. "We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down."
Anthony Albanese says the government is doing "whatever it can" to prevent a live stream of an execution in the US from being viewed in Australia.
He says social media platforms have a "social responsibility" to do the right thing and not broadcast the execution.
US President Donald Trump is yet to make the ultimate call about the December 3 execution.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says his government will do everything it can to stop the "abhorrent" live stream of a firing squad execution in the United States from being shown in Australia.

Last week US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009, would be available for the public to watch, but Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt about whether that would occur.
The potential live stream has elicited a strong response in parliament, with federal members across the political divide urging the government to "pull every single lever" to block the broadcast.
On Tuesday Mr Albanese told Afternoon Briefing that the government would do whatever it could, but acknowledged it was not as simple as "turning off a light switch".
"Australia has had a bipartisan position of opposition to the death penalty and I find the idea of live streaming the death of anybody completely abhorrent," he told ABC.
"We should do whatever we can to stop that occurring."
He said the government was seeking advice on its options.
On Monday the eSafety Commission said it could not prevent Australians from seeing the execution.

"While eSafety does not have powers to proactively prevent a live stream from occurring online, online services have responsibilities under Australia's online safety regulatory framework to protect users from harmful material," a spokesperson told the ABC.
The prime minister said he would make it "very clear" to social media platforms that the content had no place in Australia.
"I think anybody broadcasting this will damage their own reputations as well. They have a social responsibility here to do the right thing," he said.
The ABC has contacted Google, Meta and TikTok to see if they plan to restrict the content, but has not received responses.
Asked whether he had made representations to Donald Trump on the issue, Mr Albanese said the US president had indicated in the media that he was weighing the matter.
"President Trump has already said he is giving consideration to this and I hope that there is a response in the United States as well," he said.
If the broadcast goes ahead, it will mark the first time an execution in the US has been live streamed.

Greens Leader David Shoebridge grilled Foreign Minister Penny Wong over the proposed live stream during Tuesday's Question Time and asked about the "shared values" between Australia and "a government that publicly broadcasts state-sanctioned snuff films".
Senator Wong said it would be "deeply distressing for any such vision to be live streamed".
"We don't believe anyone should be confronted with it, particularly younger Australians," she said.
Senator Wong said Australians had a right to expect such content would not appear on their screens.
"We believe that platforms do have a responsibility to meet these expectations," she said.
Shadow Foreign Affairs Minister Ted O'Brien said the government needed to ensure Australians could not view the execution.
"That concerns me deeply. We cannot have young Australians watching an execution," he told Afternoon Briefing.
"That would be appalling, repugnant, and that is why we need to be looking at every possible lever to ensure that is not live streamed, if indeed it goes ahead."

Air travel can be stressful at the best of times, but imagine adding bed bugs into the mix.
Passengers on a recent flight from Australia to Italy were reportedly faced with that nightmare.
A bed bug expert says once the blood-feeding insects are onboard, it is difficult to avoid them.
Over the weekend, Australian media reported that bed bugs grounded a Qantas plane, after passengers complained of itchy bites aboard a flight from Perth to Rome on Friday.
The plane was grounded in Rome, with passengers scheduled to return to Perth given accommodation and re-booked on different flights within two days.
Qantas is still investigating the cause.

"We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue identified on a small number of economy seats," a spokesperson said.
Bed bug expert Stephen Doggett told ABC News Radio that incidents of bed bugs on flights were well-documented.
"It's not particularly common, but it does occur," he said.
"My gut feeling working on bed bugs for 25 years is that it's probably been in the plane for sometime and just simply not detected."
In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family who said they were bitten by bed bugs while on a flight from Vancouver to London.
Mr Doggett said bed bugs find their way onto flights via clothes and belongings.
"People will stay in some location, some hotel or a hostel that has bed bugs, the bed bugs get into the belongings and they're carried on the flight. It's that simple," he said.
He says the higher risk areas of the plane are where the crew sleep.
"Because they're travelling so often, they're staying in hotels just for one night, and there's a huge turnover and that's a high risk for bed bugs," he said.
"They'll get deep into the seats, into the crevices."
Qantas said it disinfected its aircraft every 50 days as part of its standard maintenance program.
But Mr Doggett said bed bugs were a hard bug to get rid of.
He said aircraft were regularly sprayed to keep certain exotic mosquitoes out of Australia, but bed bugs were a harder challenge.
"They're really hard to get rid of because they're highly resistant to insecticides and they're amongst the most resistant insects on the planet," he said.
"There's very few chemicals actually approved for use because many chemicals can damage aircraft, can damage the aluminium."
He said using a combination of a vacuum, steam and certain insecticides can be effective, but that was an expensive task.
Unfortunately, Mr Doggett says there is virtually nothing passengers can do once they are aboard a bed bug infested flight.

"There's nowhere to go, but certainly if you think you've got bed bugs, then look in the seat, look for signs of bed bugs and most importantly take photos because you could use that even in litigation against the airline," he told ABC Perth Breakfast.
He said they will hide in the crevices and the cracks of the seats.

"Sometimes you may not see bed bugs themselves, the adult bed bugs about the size and colour of an apple seed … but the juvenile stages tend to be much smaller, and they'll be a light colour green," he said.
Pope Leo XIV said Sunday he will have surgery this week to remove an early-stage nodule on his lung.
The Vatican didn’t say what type of lung surgery the pontiff will undergo, but that the “small, localized nodule” was found in his lung during recent medical tests.
He’s expected to be admitted to the hospital Tuesday morning.

A lung nodule is a small mass of tissue detected through X-ray or CT scan screening. According to the American Lung Cancer, nodules can be caused by a number of factors, including irritants such as air pollution, diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and cancer. They can also be caused by scar tissue from a previous infection.
Leo said the nodule was detected “at a very early stage.”

There are several approaches to surgery, depending on the size and location of the nodule and whether doctors suspect cancer, said Dr. Ankit Bharat, the chief of thoracic surgery at Northwestern Medicine.
Most nodules are benign, and it’s unclear whether the pope had a biopsy after the tests.
“When doctors decide to proceed directly to surgery rather than first obtaining a biopsy, it can suggest a higher level of concern on the lung scan,” Bharat said.
What to know about Pope Leo’s surgery to remove a lung nodule

Lung cancer is more treatable if caught early. The deadly cancer is most often caused by cigarette smoking, but about 20% of lung cancer cases are diagnosed in people who have never smoked or used tobacco, according to the American Cancer Society.
However, finding a nodule on a scan doesn’t confirm a cancer diagnosis, Bharat said, and the surgery will reveal more information as doctors are able to put the nodule under a microscope.
Advances in the procedures mean they are generally less invasive, and some patients begin walking within a day or two.
If the nodule is larger and more lung tissue is removed, meaning the surgery is more extensive, it may be three to four weeks before a patient is fully recovered.
“Given the pope’s age, his recovery could be slower than that of a younger, otherwise healthy patient,” Bharat said. Leo is 71.

The pontiff has a major trip scheduled to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November. It’s possible he could make the trip, doctors suggest, if the surgery is minimally invasive and there are no surprise findings. If the nodule is cancerous, doctors will determine whether he can be treated while traveling or the trip may need to be postponed.

President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” as part of the ongoing conflict. There was no confirmation from Moscow, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he heard the news through the media.
Ukrainian officials said Russia continued to attack its energy facilities. Trump made a similar announcement a month ago, only for the two sides to also continue their aerial attacks then.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” He did not elaborate further on what the ceasefire might include.
Zelenskyy said Monday that Ukraine “didn’t know about it. We learned from the media.”
He told the Warsaw Security Forum that “we do support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side, and this looks strange.”
Ukrainian officials said Russia carried out further strikes in the hours after Trump’s announcement and on Monday morning, including against an energy facility on the outskirts of Kharkiv.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Trump’s announcement of a ceasefire that “contacts are ongoing. When we have anything to say on this topic, we’ll be sure to keep you informed.”

It follows a dramatic few days in which Trump agreed to a diesel deal with the Kremlin, demanded Kyiv halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced. The shift left Kyiv and its European allies reeling.

The U.S. agreed Friday to lift sanctions on Russian fuel in a deal that Trump said would see Russia “immediately” release 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and global marketplace,” followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that.
After strong criticism from Zelenskyy, Trump said Saturday: “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals.”

Trump has sought to blame the Ukraine conflict, rather than his own assault on Iran, for a global fuel shortage that has driven diesel prices to record highs since the U.S. launched the Middle East war in February.
Zelenskyy reiterated Sunday that he was ready to halt strikes on Russian refineries if the Kremlin halts its own attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
“We are ready for energy ceasefire, not to attack energy — both sides,” he said in an interview on ABC News’ “This Week.” He added that if Russia wants an energy ceasefire, “we are open for this.”
“Don’t attack us,” he said. “Don’t kill our children. We will stop attack your diesel.”
He also told ABC News he would hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
Zelenskyy said “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to change who is leading Ukraine.
He said it is easy for Ukraine to be blamed for higher fuel prices “when everybody in the world understands [that] because of the war in [the] Middle East, the prices are rising.”
Zelenskyy was also asked on ABC News why Trump and Elon Musk blamed him for the war’s continuation.

“Because these people can’t find a key how to stop Putin, because it’s more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others, because it’s more simple to speak about the prices and connect it with Ukraine,” he responded, pointing to how the war in Iran was leading to higher fuel prices.
Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he will undergo surgery to remove an early-stage nodule on his lung.
The Vatican said the procedure was planned for this week.
“Recently, during some medical tests, doctors discovered a localized nodule in my lung,” the American pontiff, 71, said during his noon prayer at St. Peter’s Square.

“It was detected at a very early stage and is well localized,” Leo said from the window of the Apostolic Palace. “The doctors believe it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed.”
The pontiff said that surgery had already been scheduled “for the coming days” and thanked onlookers for their support.
“I entrust myself to your prayers,” he said.
The news drew applause from the thousands gathered in the square before he wished the crowd a “happy Sunday.”
Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said in a statement that “the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week.”
Leo announced the surgery at the end of his regular address, in which he appealed for an end to the war in Ukraine and the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea.
“The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war,” he said.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is known to be physically active, including weekly games of tennis.
The pontiff has a major trip scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November. It’s unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wished Leo well.
“I would like to express to the Holy Father my personal support, and that of the Italian government, as he faces this challenge in the coming days,” she said in a statement.
“The serenity and composure with which he spoke about it [today] ... are reassuring,” Meloni added.
Born Robert Francis Prevost, he became the first American pope when he was appointed in 2025.
Originally from the South Side of Chicago, he spent much of his career ministering in Peru and leading the Vatican’s powerful office of bishops.

Leo’s father, Louis Prevost, served in the Navy during World War II and worked as a superintendent of schools in the south suburbs of Chicago. His mother, Mildred Martinez Prevost, was a librarian with a master’s degree in education and two sisters who were nuns.
Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died of a stroke in April 2025 at age 88 after a long hospitalization following a number of health issues.
Djibouti shipwreck: Death toll rises to 139 as 84 remain missing
The toll rose from 109 after the bodies of 30 more people were recovered. Search and rescue efforts are continuing.
The boat was carrying 305 people from Djibouti towards Yemen when it went down near Guehere, north of Obock, in the early hours of Friday. About 82 people survived.
IOM described it as one of the deadliest shipwrecks recorded on the Eastern Route, which runs from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula.
The shipwreck comes as Djibouti deals with continued traffic in both directions.

Since 10 September, IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix has recorded more than 20,000 movements into the country from Ethiopia, as migrants keep heading for the Gulf despite the return to full-scale fighting in Yemen.
Over roughly the same period, more than 3,700 refugees have arrived from Yemen, while 539 Ethiopian migrants have come back from there.
Alexandre Coissac, IOM’s chief of mission in Djibouti, told journalists in Geneva on 6 October that the country was facing “overlapping emergencies”.

“Djibouti is therefore confronting movements in both directions,” Mr. Coissac said, adding that migrants were increasingly becoming stranded, with more than 3,000 seen along routes in Djibouti between 20 and 30 September, often without access to basic services.
“No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope.
“We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down.”
Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and recovery operations as fears grow for those still unaccounted for.
IOM is providing emergency assistance to survivors at its Migrant Response Centre in Obock, including healthcare, psychosocial support, food, shelter and protection services.
The UN Resident Coordinator in Djibouti, Jose Barahona, said he was deeply saddened by the loss of at least 139 lives, among them children.

“Our thoughts are with the victims, the survivors and the families waiting for news of their loved ones,” Mr. Barahona said on social media. “We express our solidarity and welcome the ongoing search and rescue efforts.”

Every life lost at sea is a tragedy, he added, recalling the Secretary-General’s recent warning that such deaths underline the urgency of protecting people on the move, expanding safe migration pathways and strengthening international cooperation.
Sustaining livelihoods amid crisis in Gaza

Nidaa, Hanaa and Hanin have different stories, but share a common thread: the determination to build something of their own and keep it going despite extraordinary challenges facing them in war-ravaged Gaza.
Following the devastation of the past three years, productive capacity in Gaza has been severely damaged, markets disrupted and the cost of basic goods has risen sharply.
Their experiences reflect different parts of the same challenge: sustaining livelihoods that still exist, helping businesses restart and creating new opportunities where livelihoods have disappeared.

Running a business today means navigating uncertainty at every turn. Yet amid these challenges, women continue to find ways to work, adapting their businesses, learning new skills and somehow – supporting their families.
Nidaa: A livelihood built from childhood
Nidaa, 35, has her own business raising and selling chickens, ducks and rabbits in the southern city of Khan Younis.

“I was passionate about this business since I was a child,” she said. “My mother worked with animals, and she taught me everything she knew. During the war, I faced many challenges with continuing my business. However, I insisted on continuing.”
When her home was destroyed during the war and she was displaced, she managed to save some of her animals and move them to Khan Younis.

Trained as a teacher, Nidaa chose to follow her passion for raising animals, turning it into a business that helps support her family, including two brothers with disabilities. But there have been constant challenges.
‘During the time of famine, I lost many animals’
“Especially during the time of famine, I lost many animals,” she recalled. “Food became very expensive.”
Right now, challenges include shelter for the coming winter, access to safe water and limited ingredients for food for the birds and animals, she said.
“I don’t know how I will take care of them without a proper shelter,” she said.

Through the UN Development Programme (UNDP) partnership with the local Chamber of Commerce, she received a grant to purchase animals and equipment, alongside training to strengthen her production skills.
Now, Nidaa’s ambition goes beyond sustaining what she has today.
“I hope that my business will grow,” she said, “and I can inspire other women to work with animals.”
In Gaza City, Hanaa, 49, started a family dairy business with her husband in 2021.
During the war, she lost her husband, one of her sons and her business. She was left supporting her three remaining children while also caring for five children who lost both parents.
With encouragement from her eldest son, Fouad, Hanaa decided to restart the business despite limited resources and severe shortages of milk and other raw materials.
“Sometimes, the people who need us are the reason we find the strength to keep going,” Hanaa said, adding that she chooses to remain strong and resilient in the face of many challenges.

The destruction of Gaza’s electricity system has made dairy production particularly difficult. Power interruptions can cause products to spoil, resulting in losses at a time when resources are already scarce.

With grant support, Hanaa was able to resume producing cheese, milk, labneh and laban, with hopes of growing her business into a larger production facility and build a more stable source of income for her family.
For other women, starting over begins with a new skill.
Hanin, 36, is learning carpentry. From southern Khan Younis, she travels to Deir al-Balah to complete 80 hours of vocational training, followed by entrepreneurship and business-planning training.

“This is something unique, especially for women,” Hanin said. “It’s needed now more than ever, because there are limited sources of wood for furniture, and many people lost their furniture during the war.”
More than 200 trainees will receive skills development in carpentry, textiles, recycling, compost production, data science, graphic design and digital marketing.
For Hanin, learning carpentry is not simply about completing a training course. It offers a pathway towards earning an income and potentially building a business of her own.
For women entrepreneurs, access to finance and skills is important, but their ability to sustain and grow their businesses also depends on the systems around them.
That means reliable energy and water, functioning markets and access to the equipment and materials they need.
Supporting women-led businesses is therefore about more than individual livelihoods, according to UNDP.
It also helps preserve local productive capacity, generate income and keep economic activity rooted in Palestinian communities, laying the foundation for locally driven recovery.
Nearly two million Palestinians have experienced repeated displacement since the war began. Here are some ongoing efforts to help them recover:
- Since October 2023, UNDP has supported 6,000 emergency employment opportunities

- Nidaa and Hanaa are among 30 women whose businesses are being supported as part of UNDP’s Gaza Neighbourhood Approach initiative, which brings together shelter, essential services and livelihood opportunities to help communities regain some of the basic conditions they need to function
- UNDP’s Programme of Assistance to the Palestinian People (PAPP) supports micro, small and medium enterprises with grants, equipment and skills development
- The REVIVE housing project has already helped build homes for displaced Palestinians
‘These attacks must cease immediately’: Guterres condemns deadly Houthi strike on Riyadh airport
In a short statement issued late on Saturday, he said attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law. “These attacks must cease immediately,” Mr. Guterres said.
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said on Sunday that 309 people were wounded in the strike on King Khalid International Airport, some of them critically.
The dead include at least four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, a US citizen, plus others from Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. Operations were suspended and flights diverted.
Late on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported that another projectile had hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh, causing further injuries and a fire.

It was the third Houthi attack on the airport this week. Thursday’s strikes killed three Saudis, including a Saudia pilot, and earlier attacks on King Khalid and Abha airports reportedly killed three more and wounded 36.
Houthi media reported the airport in Yemen’s capital Sana’a – which the group has controlled for years – had been hit by an airstrike on Sunday, blaming Saudi Arabia for the attack.

According to news reports, the vice-president of Yemen’s internationally recognised government called on Sunday for decisive action by regional and international partners to end the Houthi aggression.

The Iran-backed Houthis have fought the Saudi-backed government since 2014. A 2022 ceasefire largely held until this summer. In September, the Houthis swept down Yemen’s Red Sea coast, capturing the port of Mokha and islands in the Bab al-Mandab strait.

Early this month, government forces launched a counteroffensive, backed by Saudi-led air strikes, aiming to retake all Houthi-held territory – including Sana’a. The Houthis have answered with missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The battle for Bab al-Mandab, the narrow gateway to the Red Sea, is a spillover from the US-Iran conflict which has destabilised global oil and gas supplies through the vital Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
With Iran continuing to disrupt the strait, the Red Sea has become vital for Saudi oil exports.
Saudi officials and the Yemeni government say they have now regained control of the Red Sea chokepoint – but the Houthis have denied the claim.
The UN Security Council met Friday morning in New York on Yemen where Special Envoy Hans Grundberg said the country had slid back into full-scale war.
The conflict is intensifying, raising regional security and economic risks, he told amassadors.
UN Deputy Emergency Relief Coordinator Mohamed Yahya said over 200,000 people have been displaced since August, the highest new displacement since the now-shattered 2022 truce.
HELSINKI — China completed its ninth and tenth launches of September, sending Guowang and Yaogan satellites into orbit, ahead of an intense finish to the year.

A Long March 8A lifted off at 9:32 a.m. Eastern (1332 UTC) Sept. 23 from the Hainan commercial spacecraft launch site, carrying the 26th group of satellites for China’s Guowang national low Earth orbit satellite internet project. Less than a day later, a Long March 6A lifted off at 4:46 a.m. Eastern (0846 UTC) Sept. 24 from Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center with the fourth group of Yaogan-40 satellites.

The pair of launches capped a September in which Chinese launchers flew at a pace that frequently saw multiple orbital missions within days, including four different rockets launching from three sites within 48 hours Sept. 15–16.

China Aerospace Science and Technology Corp. (CASC) stated the Guowang satellites had entered their planned orbits. The satellites were later tracked by U.S. Space Force in roughly circular 1,100-kilometer-altitude orbits inclined by 50 degrees. The batch was developed under the overall leadership of the China Academy of Space Technology (CAST), CASC’s main spacecraft maker, according to the corporation.

Guowang is run by China SatNet, a state-owned enterprise established in 2021, and is planned to comprise around 13,000 satellites. The constellation uses satellites from multiple manufacturers and is launched on a range of Long March vehicles, with the Long March 8A, which debuted in February 2025, now launching regularly from Hainan’s commercial pads.

The three Yaogan-40 (04) satellites will mainly be used for electromagnetic environment detection and related technology experiments, Xinhua reported, using boilerplate language typical of Yaogan launches. The satellites were also developed under CAST’s leadership.

The satellites entered near polar orbits with altitudes of around 800 km, joining three earlier batches in similar orbits. Analysis by Integrity ISR indicates that the Yaogan-40 groups are placed into orbital planes separated by 72 degrees in right ascension of the ascending node, suggesting a fifth group will be needed to complete the constellation.

The Long March 6A, a kerosene-liquid oxygen core with solid boosters, is one of CASC’s main vehicles for both Yaogan and megaconstellation missions from Taiyuan. The rocket has now flown 27 times since its debut in March 2022, with all flights successfully reaching orbit, though the upper stage has experienced a number of breakup events after payload deployment.

The pair of launches take China to 70 orbital launch attempts for 2026. With the country aiming to surpass 100 launches in a calendar year for the first time, the final quarter will see heavy activity. China launched 26 times in Q3, following 26 in Q2 and 18 in Q1, and would need to conduct at least 31 launches in Q4. The country’s annual launch schedule is typically backloaded with a greater number of launches later in the year.

One major mission will be Shenzhou-24. China’s next crewed mission now appears likely to launch around November, using a Long March 2F from Jiuquan. The crew is expected, though not officially confirmed, to include a Pakistani payload specialist, chosen from one of two Pakistan Air Force pilots in training at the Astronaut Center of China. The selected astronaut would become the first foreign astronaut to visit Tiangong.

A press conference a day ahead of the Shenzhou-24 launch may also provide updates or insights into the schedule for the first launch of the Mengzhou new generation spacecraft and the Long March 10A, both of which are related to China’s crewed lunar plans.

Possible debut launches include Orienspace’s Gravity-2, iSpace’s Hyperbola-3 with a first stage recovery attempt, and Zhihang-1 from Zenk Space, which earlier aimed for a launch in June. These would add to 2026 debuts including Tianlong-3 (April), Kinetica-2 (March), the Long March 12B (June), Long March 10B (July) and Pallas-1 (Sept. 1).

Numerous launches for the Guowang and Qianfan constellations are expected. Other notable possible payloads in the coming months include Fengxing-1 on a Gravity-1 solid rocket, which could be China’s first commercial orbital transfer vehicle, from Future Space. Also expected are space computing payloads. The schedule for the planned debut flight of the Haolong reusable spaceplane for cargo to Tiangong from AVIC on a Zhuque-3 rocket from Landspace is currently unknown.

Galileo Space is building satellites designed to turn signals into answers in orbit. Modern defense and commercial operations need fast answers about what is happening and where. Existing systems can leave segmented data crawling through processing for hours or days. FPV drones and moving radars must be detected and tracked quickly. Ballistic missile launch plume detection can provide critical early warning. Interference disrupting navigation frequencies or crucial satcom links must be detected and traced to its source. A ship lost at sea may still broadcast a distress signal. A tumbling satellite may lose contact with the ground while still emitting signals that help locate it. Rescue crews may have only hours to find someone before nightfall.

The solution combines innovative sensors with AI fusion at the edge to generate actionable reports directly in orbit. The system is designed to operate fully autonomously for weeks, selecting and carrying out its own sensing tasks. It identifies threats, geolocates signals and delivers actionable intelligence to operators within minutes, not hours or days. The mission is to give defense teams the early warning they need to survive and commercial operators the answers they need to act.

Working side by side with government stakeholders, the team has developed a deep understanding of operational needs and critical capability gaps. The company is in the final stages of securing its first government contract. Its first demonstration satellite is scheduled to launch in Q4 of 2027 to prove its capabilities in orbit and open the door to a potential Phase III government contract. Galileo has also deepened relationships with commercial companies that need near live data, creating a path to early revenue alongside its defense business.
Galileo was selected for a16z speedrun as one of 80 companies chosen from 30,000 applicants.

CEO: Brings a decade of experience in national security space and military systems at Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin. Led testing in orbit for protected military communications satellites and consulted for the U.S. Space Force on acquiring new technology. Combines spacecraft engineering expertise with deep knowledge of defense missions, government procurement and what operators need.

CSO: Was responsible for building machine learning systems for Google, YouTube and Amazon’s Prime Video. Brings expertise in AI, software infrastructure and building systems at global scale. Now leads Galileo’s satellite software, bringing that experience into orbit to turn complex sensor data into clear intelligence that operators can act on.

CTO: Designed, tested and delivered all RF radios for SpaceX Starship flights, owning the radios through Flight 10, including first booster catch at the tower. Introduced Starship’s first integrated Starlink phased array antenna and RTK GPS receiver hardware that helped guide the booster back to the tower. Previously worked on electronic warfare for a Navy jammer missile at Raytheon and designed high power RF amplifiers for the Navy and Ka band block upconverters for the Army at two startups.

ROME, 30/09/2026 – NaviGate, an Italian space technology company spun out of Sapienza University of Rome, has successfully completed the in-orbit demonstration (IoD) of NaviCode Caravel, its autonomous onboard precise orbit determination software, aboard an ION Satellite Carrier operated by D-Orbit. During the demonstration, NaviCode Caravel ran directly on the satellite’s onboard computer, computing the spacecraft’s position in real time using only the raw data of the GNSS receiver already onboard, with no additional hardware.

Today, knowing precisely where a satellite is remains largely a ground-based activity: operators rely on dedicated infrastructure, specialized flight dynamics teams, and repeated ground contacts to accurately reconstruct and predict the orbit of each spacecraft. As constellations grow in size and missions become more responsive, this approach turns into a bottleneck in terms of cost, workload, and reaction time. NaviCode Caravel moves precise orbit determination onboard: a software-only product that transforms the raw measurements of the GNSS receiver a satellite already carries into high-accuracy, real-time knowledge of its own position, available directly where operational decisions are made. Beyond determining where the satellite is now, Caravel can also predict where it will be, together with a measure of how reliable that prediction is, giving the spacecraft the forward-looking awareness it needs to anticipate upcoming events, such as ground station contacts or payload operations, and manage them autonomously onboard.

The demonstration was carried out through D-Orbit’s Software In-Orbit Demonstration service and structured in two phases. NaviCode Caravel was first validated on the ground on an engineering model replicating the in-orbit computing environment. The application was then uploaded to an ION Satellite Carrier already in orbit and executed onboard, processing real flight telemetry from the spacecraft’s GNSS receiver across multiple runs.

The software executed nominally onboard and in real time without anomalies. Onboard positioning reached a best-case formal uncertainty of 5.2 cm, with mean values in the decimeter range across the runs, using GPS-only measurements. NaviGate then verified the onboard solutions on the ground, proving them consistent with the reference orbits reconstructed through classical ground-based precise orbit determination performed with GODOT, the European Space Agency’s flight dynamics software. NaviCode Caravel is also designed to process multi-constellation GNSS data and correction services such as SBAS and Galileo HAS, enabling even higher accuracy in operational deployments.

“Satellites still depend heavily on the ground to know exactly where they are and where they will be. NaviCode Caravel changes that: it is a software product that lets a satellite compute its own position with high accuracy, in real time, using the GNSS receiver it already carries, with no new hardware,” said Andrea Sesta, Chief Technology Officer and Co-founder at NaviGate. “Seeing it run in orbit without a single anomaly, and produce solutions consistent with the reference orbits computed on the ground, is the validation we were working toward, and a real milestone for the whole NaviGate team. D-Orbit’s Software In-Orbit Demonstration service was key to getting there quickly: we developed and tested our application on the ground in the same containerized environment used in orbit, iterated fast, and flew on real flight data within months, which is exactly what a company like ours needs to bring a flight-proven product to market.”

“With five networked Intelligence Nodes in orbit, we can give customers access to space infrastructure that is already up and running. For NaviGate, that means testing their precise orbit determination algorithms ingesting raw GNSS measurements and attitude telemetry in real time from D-Orbit’s ION platform, in-situ directly on-board, with no satellite to develop or launch. It’s a practical way to move from simulation to real flight data in less time and at lower cost,” said Viney Jean-Francois Dhiri, Head of Growth, Sales and Marketing of the Space Cloud Business Unit at D-Orbit.

Caravel is the first release of the NaviCode fleet: subsequent versions will extend these capabilities to multi-sensor resilient navigation and to autonomous maneuver planning for large constellations. NaviCode Caravel was also selected as a winner of the CASSINI Challenges 2026, the European Union’s space entrepreneurship competition run by the EU Agency for the Space Programme (EUSPA).

The in-orbit demonstration is the culminating milestone of the proof-of-concept program funded by Galaxia, the Italian Technology Transfer Hub on Aerospace powered by CDP Venture Capital together with Obloo Ventures, which backed NaviGate from its earliest stage. NaviGate was founded by researchers who developed deep expertise in spacecraft navigation and precise orbit determination through their work on ESA and NASA missions, and originated as a spin-off of Sapienza University of Rome.

Following the demonstration, NaviGate is engaging constellation operators and mission integrators for the first pilot deployments. NaviCode Caravel addresses concrete needs across the market: reducing the ground workload and infrastructure required for precise orbit determination in constellation operations, enhancing onboard image processing for Earth observation missions, supporting PNT constellations, and improving orbit knowledge for launch vehicles and orbital transfer applications, with further applications across other mission types and orbital regimes.

Spun out of Sapienza University of Rome, NaviGate S.r.l. is an Italian space technology startup founded by researchers with extensive experience in spacecraft navigation and precise orbit determination across ESA and NASA missions including Juno, Cassini, Veritas, BepiColombo, and JUICE, and initiatives such as ESA Moonlight and Marconi constellations. The company develops NaviCode, a modular, data-agnostic software platform that enables satellites and constellations to perform precise orbit determination, orbit prediction, and autonomous maneuvering without continuous ground intervention, leveraging GNSS, radiometric, optical, and other navigation measurements. NaviGate was incorporated in 2026 and is backed by Galaxia, Italy’s national technology transfer hub for aerospace, and supported by the ESA BIC Lazio incubation program.
More information on www.navigate-space.com

Its ION Satellite Carrier is an orbital transfer vehicle (OTV) used for satellite deployment and hosted payload operations; since 2020 it has flown 23 missions and carried 240+ payloads, including hosted payloads and satellites deployed in orbit. The company also provides space cloud services based on onboard computing for in-orbit data processing and is developing GEA, a servicing spacecraft intended to support autonomous rendezvous, inspection, and refueling, as well as NOX, a synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) Earth observation satellite.
